guides.title: The essentials for your first account.
guides.summary: Find the main screens, establish usable production and plan the time you will be away.
guides.label: Guide and reference
guides.status: Foundations reviewed 9 November 2026. Current costs and prerequisites remain subject to the in-game technology tree.
objectives: Find production, construction, research, fleet and event information.
Complete and check one small economic upgrade without breaking your energy balance.
Separate an account class, a planet’s lifeform and a play style.
Plan your next login before leaving ships or resources behind.

sections.title: Know what you are managing
paragraphs: OGame is a persistent game: production, timers and fleet movements continue while you are away. Your account is a network of planets and, later, moons. You spend Metal, Crystal and Deuterium on mines, facilities, research, ships and defenses. Energy supports production; it is not a resource you can load into a cargo ship.

Start by finding the selected planet, your resource balances, the event list and the server clock. Open Resources to inspect mines and power, Facilities for supporting buildings, Research for technologies and Fleet for dispatch. Names and positions can differ between desktop and mobile interfaces. Before buying something, open its details and technology prerequisites. A disabled button often means a requirement is missing, not that the page is broken.

sections.title: Early production and its constraints
steps: A useful mine upgrade needs its resource cost and supporting energy. Solar Plant is a straightforward early source; the energy reference compares the later alternatives.
Metal and Crystal support the construction loop. Deuterium becomes important for research, ships and fuel. Preserve resources for the prerequisite that enables the next useful capability.
The limiting resource and next unlock matter more than a fixed mine ratio. Include power, storage, transport and the remaining construction time in the comparison.
After completion, compare the level, power balance and hourly output under unchanged bonus settings. A nominal production upgrade is not delivering its full benefit if energy or storage blocks it.

callout.title: A comparison method, not a fixed 10/8/6 build
callout.text: A fixed mine ratio can be a rough reference, but universe speed, rewards, existing levels and your next unlock change the useful order. The economy guide explains how to compare the actual next level on each mine.

links.title: Mine formulas, costs and marginal returns

sections.title: Use the technology tree as your map
paragraphs: Pick the first capability you need: move resources, explore, settle another planet or progress research. Open that item’s technology details and work backward through the prerequisites. Build only the missing facilities and research levels needed for that near-term goal. A mine makes income; a laboratory or shipyard enables something else. Judge each on the job it performs.

Once you have cargo ships, practise a small transport between suitable owned locations before depending on a large shipment. Confirm the mission, destination type, fuel, payload and return time. Transport does not station the fleet permanently. Read the fleetsaving guide before treating any dispatch as safe storage.

Early rewards and tutorials can accelerate progression. Read what a reward does before claiming or spending it, and do not build a permanent strategy around a temporary event. More stored resources also require a plan to keep them from becoming an easy target.

sections.title: Class, lifeform and play style are different
paragraphs: Collector, Discoverer and General are account classes with different bonuses. Lifeform species are chosen on planets and unlock their own buildings; Lifeform technologies are another layer again. A miner is a play style, not a requirement to choose one species everywhere. An expedition player still needs mines, cargo, power and fleet safety.

You do not need to settle every advanced choice immediately. Establish production and a reliable routine, then choose the miner, expedition or active-fleet path that fits the time you will actually spend playing. The play-style pages give a investment priorities and explain when to postpone an upgrade.

sections.title: End the session before closing the game
steps: Read all active fleet events and queued ship completions. Note what will arrive or finish while you are away.

Estimate the unconstrained stock at your next login: current stock plus hourly production multiplied by hours away. Then check when each storage fills, because mine production stops at that limit. Include known deliveries, rewards and queued spending separately.
Keep flight fuel and transport capacity available. Do not spend your entire reserve on a last-minute upgrade.
Follow the fleetsaving guide for ships and movable resources you cannot afford to lose. Defense is a deterrent, not a substitute for a safe fleet return.
Choose a realistic next login and one objective for that visit. A sustainable routine is more valuable than a plan that requires you to watch timers all night.

If the actual increase differs from the estimate, inspect energy, storage, production settings and bonus expiry. The economy reference gives worked examples for both upgrades and the next storage deadline.

sections.title: Know what each mine does
sections.body: Mines provide recurring Metal, Crystal and Deuterium while power and storage permit. Compare the next level’s additional output, not the planet’s total income. Temperature, position and active bonuses can change the useful choice.

sections.title: Early production and infrastructure
sections.body: Early growth needs both production and the facilities for a useful unlock. Fund the missing resource and its supporting power rather than copying a fixed mine ratio. The detailed reference keeps the first-planet checklist.

sections.title: Measure before you spend
sections.body: Read current production, power, storage and fields on each candidate planet. Keep the same class, universe speed and active bonuses in both sides of a comparison. A shortage of power or collection capacity is not solved by another mine.

sections.title: Name the next constraint
sections.body: The limiting resource is the one that delays the intended purchase longest. Use current stock and reliable net production, then include deliveries at their actual arrival times. Reserve flight fuel and check infrastructure before spending.

sections.title: Compare the complete investment
sections.body: Simple payback divides the complete project cost by its extra net income. Include supporting power and operating fuel, use consistent resource values, and compare across planets. A shorter payback can still lose to an urgent unlock or resource constraint.

sections.title: Make the offline interval affordable
sections.body: Current stock plus production during your absence is an unconstrained forecast. A full store stops further mine accumulation. Price storage against production actually saved, and include known deliveries and spending separately. More storage does not make a stockpile safe.

sections.title: Verify the result
sections.body: After completion, compare actual output under the same settings. Check energy, storage, production sliders and bonus expiry if the gain differs. Keep one funded improvement, one next target and enough reserves to protect the operation.

objectives: Understand why a flying fleet still needs a safe return.

sections.title: Protect the return, not only the departure
sections.body: A flying fleet still needs a protected landing. Choose a time you can cover, allow for reconnecting and reading events, and use the current dispatch display. Defense does not make an unattended valuable fleet safe.

sections.title: Choose a method you understand
sections.body: Outbound Deployment is visible at its destination planet, not its origin; recalled Deployment is absent from phalanx. Moon destinations avoid a directly scannable endpoint, but moon destruction and prior observation still matter. Transport has different return visibility.

sections.title: Run the departure checklist
sections.body: Check ships, destination type, mission, speed, cargo, fuel and arrival before sending. Then verify the movement in the event list. Outstanding returns and new shipyard completions can leave valuable ships behind after an otherwise correct departure.

sections.title: Plan around real life
sections.body: Match the route to your real availability and connection reliability. A narrow alarm window is not a safety margin. Vacation mode has conditions and should not be assumed to fix an already developing attack.

sections.title: Recall timing and threat response
sections.body: Understand recall timing with a small fleet before relying on it. When threatened, read the actual mission and timing before changing the route. A recall or moon loss can change the return plan; obtain private, situation-specific help rather than publishing live fleet details.

guides.title: Turn a new colony into a useful planet.
guides.summary: Choose a useful location and budget capacity, the colony ship, startup resources and logistics together.
guides.label: Topic overview
guides.status: Evidence reviewed 9 November 2026. Read the linked reference for formulas, sources and version limits; current account settings remain the final check.
objectives: Choose a colony for an explicit role.
Budget the full expansion rather than only the ship.
Evaluate fields, logistics and safety after arrival.

sections.title: Decide what the colony is for
sections.body: A colony can add production, shorten supply routes or open another operating area. Choose the job before the position. Research capacity, a Colony Ship, startup resources, fuel and ongoing logistics all belong in the expansion budget.

sections.title: Check capacity and prerequisites
sections.body: Planet capacity and access to a particular position are separate checks. Confirm both in Astrophysics and the technology tree before launch. The Colony Ship’s prerequisites and the relevant capacity thresholds are covered in the detailed reference.

sections.title: Compare candidate locations
sections.body: Position affects production bonuses, temperature and possible size. Cold planets improve Deuterium production but weaken satellites. Temperature does not change Solar Plant output. The reference compares slot 8 and slot 15 under stated assumptions.

sections.title: Compare all fifteen positions
sections.body: The fifteen-position table separates unmodified field ranges, possible maximum temperatures and production bonuses. A range is not a guaranteed colony roll. Universe, class, item and Lifeform field effects must be applied separately.

sections.title: Apply field bonuses in the right place
sections.body: Colonization diameter bonuses are not the same as field bonuses: fields depend on diameter squared. Keep a long-term space budget and check effects that can disappear after a species change. Position production bonuses also have their own place in the calculation.

sections.title: Inspect before heavily investing
sections.body: Inspect the actual fields, temperature and location before committing a large development budget. Accompanying ships normally return after a colonization delivery; use a separate Deployment to station cargo. Abandoning a colony needs its own careful asset and warning check.

sections.title: Develop in stages and connect the route
sections.body: A useful colony needs powered income, the facilities for its chosen job, cargo and a reliable collection route. Supply it in manageable amounts without starving the rest of the account. Judge expansion by its contribution and operating burden together.

guides.title: Research toward a useful unlock.
guides.summary: Choose a usable capability or recurring benefit, with the right prerequisites and eligible laboratories.
guides.label: Topic overview
guides.status: Evidence reviewed 9 November 2026. Read the linked reference for formulas, sources and version limits; current account settings remain the final check.
objectives: Trace prerequisites backward from a goal.
Separate unlocks from incremental improvements.
Schedule research around the rest of the account.

sections.title: Start with a capability
sections.body: Start from a capability you will use or recurring income you can measure. Include every missing building and technology prerequisite. The reference compares Plasma, Astrophysics, drives, cargo and other research by their actual effects.

sections.title: Classify the benefit
sections.body: Classic research applies across the account. Lifeform technology levels are local investments whose applicable active bonuses can contribute account-wide. Unlocks, capacity, efficiency and prerequisites answer different needs; a classic research queue does not create parallel research.

sections.title: Research costs and prerequisites
sections.body: Price the whole chain and reserve the resources for the next usable result. Extra fleet or expedition capacity earns nothing when you cannot fund or operate it. Compare the full completion date, not an isolated technology timer.

sections.title: Buy time deliberately
sections.body: Laboratory investment pays in time saved on a research program you can fund. Intergalactic Research Network combines eligible labs, not every lab automatically. Use the published total research-speed multiplier once rather than multiplying economy speed twice.

sections.title: Test the unlocked capability
sections.body: Confirm the new capability and revise affected plans after research finishes. Drive upgrades can change fleetsave times; capacity needs ships and attention; production improvements need a like-for-like comparison. Reassess the next bottleneck instead of buying another level by habit.

guides.title: Choose power for the demand you have.
guides.summary: Compare solar, satellites and fusion through useful power, fuel cost, fields and resilience.
guides.label: Topic overview
guides.status: Evidence reviewed 9 November 2026. Read the linked reference for formulas, sources and version limits; current account settings remain the final check.
objectives: Calculate solar and fusion output on the same baseline.
Understand why Energy Technology improves every reactor.
Plan a transition without losing mine production.

sections.title: Compare three different power sources
sections.body: Solar Plants provide durable power without fuel. Satellites save fields but are vulnerable and temperature-dependent. Fusion offers dense, durable output at a Deuterium operating cost. The best mix depends on the demand, resources and infrastructure you already have.

sections.title: Understand the scaling
sections.body: Fusion output depends on reactor level and account-wide Energy Technology. Economy speed scales baseline fuel consumption, not energy output. Energy Technology does not raise Solar Plant or satellite output. Exact formulas and display-rounding assumptions are in the reference.

sections.title: Read the worked comparison
sections.body: The full-output comparison separates generated energy, fields and hourly fuel at ×1 and ×8 economy. It establishes output and field efficiency, not equal-cost superiority. Use the seven-row worked table before pricing an actual transition.

sections.title: Why the same reactor becomes better
sections.body: A shared Energy Technology upgrade can benefit several reactors, while a reactor upgrade helps one planet. At a common demand, compare total support costs and the resources retained after fuel. Spare power alone is not the financial benefit.

sections.title: Switch in a controlled sequence
sections.body: Keep existing production powered until replacement supply works. Compare net Deuterium and the next mine or crawler demand, retain recovery capacity, and verify any partial reactor setting in the resource screen. The reference preserves a transition checklist.

sections.title: The decision rule
sections.body: Prefer a system that meets useful demand with affordable construction, sustainable fuel and acceptable exposure. Existing solar, fusion and a modest satellite reserve can coexist. Do not demolish working infrastructure solely because a fresh-build calculation favors another option.

guides.title: Make crawlers earn their power bill.
guides.summary: Separate owned count, working capacity and realized production, then compare normal operation with Collector overload.
guides.label: Topic overview
guides.status: Evidence reviewed 9 November 2026. Read the linked reference for formulas, sources and version limits; current account settings remain the final check.
objectives: Calculate the mine-based active crawler limit.
Separate Collector output, Geologist capacity and overload.
Check net income after energy costs and production caps.

sections.title: Understand what you are buying
sections.body: Crawlers are stationary, vulnerable production support. Their construction prerequisites, unit cost and class requirement belong in the project budget. Begin with reliable mines and power, and do not treat them as ships that can accompany a fleetsave.

sections.title: Calculate the working limit
sections.body: Keep owned count, permitted working count and realized production separate. Mine levels set baseline working capacity; Collector, Geologist and Lifeform effects can change the result. The documented 50% production-cap repair is July 2026 PTS evidence, not a new live-universe measurement.

sections.title: Work through one planet
sections.body: The 30/25/25 mine example separates 640 base working crawlers from 704 with baseline Collector and Geologist capacity. Its comparison table excludes Lifeform effects and shows the different production and energy consequences of Collector overload.

sections.title: Stop before extra spending stops helping
sections.body: A working-count increase need not increase income at a production ceiling. Do not buy or power a batch that produces no useful extra output. The exact complete Lifeform crawler interaction remains unverified, so check the account’s actual bonus row.

sections.title: Measure the marginal return
sections.body: Overload increases energy demand faster than crawler output. Compare additional Metal, Crystal and Deuterium retained after supplying that power, including additional fusion fuel. The reference provides six workload rows and a marginal net-income example.

sections.title: Add crawlers in verified batches
sections.body: Verify one planet before repeating an investment. Check count, energy and final output at the intended workload. Recalculate after mine upgrades, class changes, Geologist expiry or Lifeform changes, and keep a replacement and power-recovery reserve.

guides.title: Expeditions
guides.summary: Build a replaceable fleet around the reward limit, cargo capacity and launches you can actually maintain.
guides.label: Topic overview
guides.status: Evidence reviewed 9 November 2026. Read the linked reference for formulas, sources and version limits; current account settings remain the final check.
objectives: Identify the inputs behind an expedition fleet.
Avoid mistaking long holding time for larger rewards.
Measure net results and operational risk.

sections.title: What an expedition actually does
sections.body: Expeditions travel to position 16, hold, resolve a random event and return surviving ships. They need both expedition allowance and a free ordinary fleet slot. Their value depends on the launches you can sustain, not just the size of one find.

sections.title: Build the slot count correctly
sections.body: Astrophysics provides the baseline allowance; class, Admiral and items can add slots. Ordinary fleet slots remain a separate limit. The detailed table distinguishes the additions and the capacity that may disappear when a bonus expires.

sections.title: Record the account you are calculating for
sections.body: Use your class, universe settings, top-player bracket, active bonuses and current game version. October Orion test notes changed non-Discoverer economy scaling; the later live notices do not independently settle activation on every older universe. Do not assume one recipe applies everywhere.

sections.title: Separate reward value from cargo capacity
sections.body: Expedition points qualify fleet value for a reward bracket; cargo carries the resources home. More ships beyond the useful threshold do not indefinitely increase rewards. Base Metal-plus-Crystal cost defines the classic points, not Armour Technology.

sections.title: Build a replaceable working fleet
sections.body: Choose cargo and support ships for their specific effects, with enough reserves to replace a lost launch. A Pathfinder’s multiplier does not repeatedly double with more Pathfinders. Advanced Deathstar composition changes combat-event exposure but does not remove black-hole risk.

sections.title: Fleet verification before expansion
sections.body: Review the complete schedule and preserve ordinary transport and fleetsave capacity. Verify a working composition, its reports and delayed returns before expanding it across the available slots. A fleet you cannot replace is too large for a routine gamble.

sections.title: Avoid the two common scheduling traps
sections.body: Longer holding time changes event chance, not the maximum resource reward, and can increase delays. Depletion and practical round-trip time also matter. Compare actual launches per day rather than rewarding a longer hold by assumption.

sections.title: Keep a simple performance log
sections.body: Record resources, fuel, losses, delays and launches over a meaningful period. Keep ship finds separate from immediately spendable resources unless you have a realistic conversion use. Use net returns and an explicit valuation basis.

sections.title: Change one thing at a time
sections.body: Change the bottleneck your reports identify: value, cargo, slots, cycle time or replacement funding. Recalculate after class, bracket or major bonus changes. One exceptional reward or loss is not enough evidence for a new fleet recipe.

sections.title: Three separate choices
paragraphs: A planet’s species determines its Lifeform buildings. Population unlocks research slots. Each slot holds a technology with levels bought on that planet; eligible active contributions combine across the account. A technology’s origin species need not match the species living on the planet.

Choose for the income or fleet you actually use. Rock’tal buildings can support an expedition research selection, for example. All Lifeform buildings use zero ordinary planet fields; population, food, cost and time are the relevant constraints.

sections.title: Discovery and activation
paragraphs: For a Human discovery pilot, the Research Centre requires Residential Sector 21 and Biosphere Farm 22. Construct it, support the population and wait for the first slot. Intergalactic Envoys level 1 enables discovery missions from the Galaxy view DNA icons, not position-16 expeditions. Keep it active somewhere before replacing the pilot’s species or slot selection.

A large housing capacity is not the same as actual, sustainably fed population. Higher tiers require conversion buildings; a population shortfall can deactivate research. Stop at the next useful slot rather than funding all eighteen by default.

callout.title: Discovery limits after transfers: announced change, not a confirmed rollout
callout.text: Gameforge’s 5 November 2026 announcement, checked 9 November: a transferred or merged account can be blocked from discoveries when its carried-over mission count exceeds the destination server’s age-based limit. Gameforge plans a one-time adjustment of affected counters to the current limit, without removing previous discoveries. It also plans to remove the discovery limit on servers older than one year; servers up to one year old keep their limit. The announced rollout window is November, before Orion’s global release, but this notice does not confirm an exact deployment date. Treat these as pending changes, not rules already active in your universe. After a move, check your discovery counter and the official update before budgeting artefacts or resetting a lifeform tier. A history count higher than the adjusted counter is expected after the fix.

sections.title: Before a large upgrade
items: Budget population infrastructure, prerequisites, the desired research levels and artefacts together. Technology selection costs are 200 / 400 / 600 artefacts for tiers 1 / 2 / 3, separate from resource research costs.

Options in the same slot compete. Record the whole tier before resetting, and check the current warnings and costs. A species switch preserves developed levels for reuse but the replacement setup must support its own active research.
Test the intended setup on one suitable planet. Compare actual account-bonus changes and keep the ordinary economy, cargo and fleetsave reserve funded.

guides.title: Moonshots and moon development
guides.summary: Prepare the battle, recovery budget and first useful buildings before buying a moonshot.
guides.label: Topic overview
guides.status: Evidence reviewed 9 November 2026. Read the linked reference for formulas, sources and version limits; current account settings remain the final check.
objectives: Calculate the ships required for a baseline moonshot in your universe.
Plan the battle, debris recovery and follow-up construction before the attempt.
Budget Lunar Base fields without blocking the next upgrade.
Explain why a moon improves fleet safety but does not make parked ships safe.

sections.title: Choose the job before choosing the location
sections.body: A moon is a separate location with its own ships, resources and facilities. Choose a useful hub or operating route, then budget development as well as creation. It cannot be settled with a Colony Ship.

sections.title: Size the battle for the universe you play
sections.body: A conventional full-base shot targets 2,000,000 qualifying debris from that battle. Required ships depend on the universe’s debris setting and actual losses. Events and Lifeforms can alter the displayed chance; the full debris and Light Fighter table is in the reference.

sections.title: Prepare a controlled moonshot
sections.body: Agree the exact shot, timing, recycler recovery and lawful compensation before committing resources. Simulate the actual defending force and remove unrelated valuables. Friendly coordination does not override community rules or make a moon guaranteed.

sections.title: Read events and Lifeforms separately
sections.body: Check current event terms separately from Lifeform effects. Kaelesh’s Supra Refractor affects new-moon creation and size, not an existing moon. Exact combined stacking remains qualified. Paid M.O.O.N.S. items have different debris handling from ordinary player-arranged shots.

sections.title: Reserve the field that creates the next fields

sections.body: Develop a small working base, then the tool the location needs. Robotics saves construction time; Phalanx adds information; a Jump Gate needs another completed gate to be useful. The reference includes costs and a field-safe sequence, not a universal optimum.

sections.body: A moon has no ordinary mine economy. Deliver construction resources, scan fuel and flight fuel explicitly to the moon destination type. Use Transport for a delivery with returning ships, or Deployment to station them.

sections.title: Protect the routine, not just the moon
sections.body: Moons cannot be directly phalanxed, but parked fleets can be attacked and moons can be destroyed. Loss can redirect movements to a planet. The March 2026 fixed speed for Moon Destruction missions is distinct from other Deathstar mission speeds.

guides.title: Jump Gates and Sensor Phalanx
guides.summary: Move ships between your own moons and understand what a scan can reveal.
guides.label: Topic overview
guides.status: Evidence reviewed 9 November 2026. Read the linked reference for formulas, sources and version limits; current account settings remain the final check.
objectives: Prepare and verify an instant transfer between two of your moons.
Plan fuel and cooldowns without confusing a jump with a fleetsave.
Calculate unmodified phalanx coverage and recognise class, Lifeform and circular-system modifiers.
Identify scan visibility at each end of a mission.

sections.title: Unlock each tool for a specific job
sections.body: Sensor Phalanx and Jump Gate are moon facilities with different jobs. Check the exact prerequisites, including Hyperspace Technology rather than Hyperspace Drive for gates. Price the intended operating capability, not facilities simply because they are available.

sections.title: Use a Jump Gate without stranding the fleet
sections.body: A Jump Gate transfers ships instantly between eligible owned moons, without carrying resources. Put flight fuel at the destination in advance, confirm both gates are ready, and inspect the transferred and remaining ships afterward.

sections.title: Use the current cooldown, not an old wiki shortcut
sections.body: Both endpoints enter cooldown. Use their displayed ready timers; published player measurements are observations rather than a complete official formula. The updated description’s maximum effective gate level is 9, superseding the older level-15 claim.

sections.title: Run a scan with a question in mind
sections.body: Phalanx scans cost Deuterium at the scanning moon and reveal eligible movement information at a planet. Read mission, endpoints and arrival together. A scan is a snapshot, not continuous tracking or proof that an absent movement never existed.

sections.title: Calculate the basic coverage
sections.body: Baseline range is Phalanx level squared minus one systems to either side, within the same galaxy. Level 1 covers the local system. Class and Lifeform modifiers are separate; the reference includes the range table and coverage example.

sections.title: Ask which planet can be scanned
sections.body: Visibility depends on both mission and endpoint. Outbound Deployment appears at the destination planet; recalled Deployment is absent from phalanx. Other returns to a planet can remain visible. Consult the complete matrix before relying on a route.

sections.title: Account for the map and temporary restrictions
sections.body: Circular systems can wrap coverage within a galaxy; circular galaxies do not make phalanx cross a galaxy boundary. Temporary combat restrictions can also stop a scan. Investigate a failed action before interpreting it as a fleet change.

sections.title: Build an operating routine around the tools
sections.body: Keep local fuel, ready gates and supervised returns in one plan. Include cargo returning from moon supplies. Gate mobility does not protect a stationary fleet or replace a dependable fleetsave route.

guides.title: Nanites and missiles
guides.summary: Buy construction throughput when time is scarce; stock missiles for a defined threat.
guides.label: Topic overview
guides.status: Evidence reviewed 9 November 2026. Read the linked reference for formulas, sources and version limits; current account settings remain the final check.
objectives: Distinguish construction throughput from resource production.
Compare a Nanite upgrade with the queues it will accelerate.
Calculate a legal mix of Anti-Ballistic and Interplanetary Missiles.
Check range, interception and irreversible launch consequences before firing.

sections.title: Unlock the capability you actually need
sections.body: Nanite Factories and Missile Silos are local planetary facilities. Buy the capability needed at that location, including prerequisites and resource costs. A planet’s Nanite does not accelerate its moon or another planet.

sections.title: What a Nanite Factory accelerates
sections.body: Nanite levels halve standard local building, ship and defense production time. They do not directly raise mine income or speed classic research. Queue conflicts, including relevant Lifeform work, can prevent the upgrade or another job from starting.

sections.title: Read a baseline construction calculation
sections.body: Baseline build time uses Metal-plus-Crystal cost, the applicable Robotics or Shipyard level, completed Nanites and economy speed. Whole-second and minimum-duration rules matter for fast units. The reference preserves the four-row timing example and its exclusions.

sections.title: Buy time when time is the bottleneck
sections.body: Price a Nanite against the funded work it will accelerate, including the upgrade interval and blocked queues. Shorter timers have little immediate value while resources keep the queue empty. Keep emergency ships and ABMs available during the construction window.

sections.title: Reserve capacity for both missile types
sections.body: Silos provide capacity shared by ABMs and IPMs. One ABM occupies one unit and one IPM two; reserve defensive stock before buying offensive missiles. Capacity is not range, and consumed interceptors must be replaced.

sections.title: Know what missiles destroy and what stops them
sections.body: Each ABM intercepts one IPM. Surviving IPMs damage defense rather than fleets or buildings, ignore shields and do not allow normal defense rebuilding. Use a current missile simulation with the target’s technologies and chosen primary defense.

sections.title: Separate missile range from travel time
sections.body: Impulse Drive sets baseline missile range within a galaxy; current settings govern travel. Circular systems can change distance. Archived timing constants are qualified, so check the actual launch display rather than planning a timed strike from an old formula alone.

sections.title: Run a final check before launch
sections.body: Confirm target type, stock, range, recent defenses and interception cost before launch. An IPM cannot be recalled. Recheck the report and the target after impact instead of repeating a salvo on stale assumptions.

guides.title: Defense planning
guides.summary: Protect normal accumulation and production assets without mistaking a bunker for a fleetsave.
guides.label: Topic overview
guides.status: Evidence reviewed 9 November 2026. Read the linked reference for formulas, sources and version limits; current account settings remain the final check.
objectives: Set a defensive budget from your collection interval and realistic local threats.
Choose units for a job instead of copying a universal defense ratio.
Separate combat losses, repaired units and permanent attrition.
Check missile protection, combat bonuses and debris settings before trusting a simulation.

sections.title: Make the routine raid unattractive
sections.body: Defense should make attacks on the resources and ships you normally leave behind unattractive. It is not a substitute for fleetsaving. Start with the likely attacker, exposed value and the amount of permanent loss you can afford.

sections.title: Read the universe before choosing a build
sections.body: Debris rules, repair settings, fleet speeds and current bonuses change the value of the same defense. Write these assumptions beside the comparison. Advice from another universe can give the wrong answer even with an identical unit mix.

sections.title: Give each part of the defense a job
sections.body: Cheap targets, larger guns and shield domes serve different roles. Their useful mix depends on the attacking fleet, technologies and budgets. The detailed unit-role table supports a comparison, not a fixed defense ratio for every account.

sections.title: Understand rapid fire before adding more fodder
sections.body: Rapid fire can make a large number of cheap targets less protective than it looks. Test the actual attacker against the proposed mix. More fodder does not automatically improve the result when it gives the attacker favorable repeat shots.

sections.title: Shields protect their own unit
sections.body: Shields belong to individual units and interact with shot size and combat rules. Do not pool all shield values into a single barrier. The reference separates the published threshold rule from unresolved exact-equality behavior.

sections.title: Count permanent losses after reconstruction
sections.body: Winning a battle and preserving investment are different results. Count losses after the applicable rebuilding chance, while recognizing that expected repair is not a guaranteed outcome. Restored defenses must also face any following wave.

sections.title: Protect the bunker from missile preparation
sections.body: ABMs can intercept IPMs, but the reserve is consumed. Missile preparation can remove defenses permanently before a fleet arrives. Do not assume a guaranteed mixed-defense spillover order or that a large Silo alone means enough interception stock.

sections.title: Use missile formulas as estimates, not launch guarantees
sections.body: Weapons, Armour, interception and the selected defense target affect missile damage. Treat baseline formulas as estimates and validate the current launch. Range, travel time and damage are separate calculations.

sections.title: Develop defense by measured need
sections.body: Compare complete defense projects at a fixed resource budget, then build the smallest useful improvement. Include exposed resources, likely fleets and rebuilding reserves. A defense that wins an unrealistic test may still attract profitable routine raids.

sections.title: Make the simulator answer the real question
sections.body: Hold the attacker and budget constant, then vary uncertain technology, loot, debris recovery and repeated waves. Distinguish defender survival from attacker profitability. Record the assumptions and permanent losses rather than only a green victory result.

sections.title: When an attack is already coming
sections.body: Read the incoming mission, timing and available resources before acting. Protect movable value and coordinate privately where useful. Panic spending or a blind missile response can add cost without changing the actual threat.

sections.title: Detailed reference
sections.body: A reusable way to test a bunker without inventing a universal ratio.

guides.title: Miner play style
guides.summary: Build dependable income with efficient upgrades and a collection routine that fits your life.
guides.label: Guide and reference
guides.status: Play-style decisions reviewed 9 November 2026. Compare the current universe, class and active bonuses; examples are conditional planning comparisons.
objectives: Prioritize economic upgrades without ignoring energy, cargo or fleet safety.
Use a Rock’tal-oriented building plan as a candidate, not an automatic empire-wide switch.
Compare mine, crawler, energy and lifeform investments on the same net-income basis.

sections.title: Choose the routine before the bonuses
sections.body: This path fits an account whose income should keep arriving when the player cannot repeatedly launch expeditions or hunt targets. Collector is the natural class to compare for production and crawler support, but choose it against your current bonuses and real activity. A class switch has a cost and can alter logistics. A few excellent expedition days do not prove that a permanently active schedule will suit you.

callout.title: Passive income still needs collection
callout.text: Mines do not need relaunching, but storage fills, ships return and resources become targets. The miner routine is less click-intensive, not unattended.

sections.title: Make every existing planet productive
steps: Audit each planet’s next mine level, available energy, storage window and collection route. Fix a production shortage before buying more capacity that cannot run.
Compare the next useful mine upgrades across planets. Include supporting energy and the resource that limits your current account goal.
Maintain cargo and flight fuel for regular collection. Leave enough capacity to protect your stock between visits.
Expand a weak colony in manageable batches. Do not spend all available resources bringing every planet to the same arbitrary level if a smaller plan has better return.
sections.body: Use the economy guide’s incremental payback method. Resource weights must be consistent across cost and extra net production. If you value Deuterium differently because of trading or a fuel goal, state that assumption instead of hiding it inside the result.

sections.title: Solve the power and crawler system together
paragraphs: Crawlers connect production directly to power demand. Before filling the active crawler limit, check the next batch’s actual energy requirement and net mine gain. If you need additional fusion, include the reactor cost and operating Deuterium. If you need satellites, account for their vulnerability and your ability to rebuild power after a raid.

Read the fusion table before deciding that more Solar Plant levels are always the cheapest option. Higher Energy Technology improves fusion output across the account. At a fixed energy demand it may allow lower reactor utilization and less fuel consumption. Research is an empire-wide purchase; compare its effect across every reactor that will benefit, not just the planet you happen to be viewing.

After any crawler or energy change, compare final total production and net Deuterium with the old setup. The attractive number is the additional income you keep after supplying the power, not only the displayed percentage boost.

sections.title: Develop a production lifeform plan
paragraphs: Rock’tal is a candidate for its mining-focused buildings. Start with one planet, identify the next useful population slot and price the housing, food, tier infrastructure and technology together. Reaching a distant slot is not automatically better than improving an affordable technology you already have.

Choose production, energy or cost-saving technologies for the job you need. The selected species determines local buildings; available Lifeform technologies are not restricted to that species after discovery. Use the Lifeforms guide to compare named options and keep Intergalactic Envoys active where needed for continued discovery.

Spread early, economical research levels where they are affordable rather than chasing one very high local level without comparison. Compare the cost of unlocking another planet’s slot against the gain from a higher level on an established planet. A reset or species switch can interrupt the current setup, so plan it deliberately instead of converting every planet at once.

sections.title: Run one investment queue, not four competing ones

example.title: Illustrative priority decision
example.text: A mine project costs 12 million planning units and adds 300,000 net per day: 40 days. A crawler-plus-power project costs 9 million and adds 300,000: 30 days. The crawler project wins this simple comparison, unless it consumes fuel or Crystal reserved for a more important near-term unlock. Include the same resource weights and supporting costs on both sides.

sections.body: Keep a short queue: one funded improvement, one next target and one optional alternative. Recheck after class changes, new colonies or an expiring bonus. Keep a reserve for transport, energy recovery and fleet safety. A miner with a fragile logistics chain can lose more in one neglected return than a carefully chosen upgrade earns in weeks.
paragraphs: Use one investment shortlist across mines, Plasma, Astrophysics and colony development, crawlers with power, and Lifeform production improvements. Compare their additional net income over the same period and at the same resource values. Research can benefit the whole account; a local upgrade benefits one planet. A temporary resource shortage or a practical collection constraint can reasonably change the order.

sections.title: Size storage and cargo for the next absence
paragraphs: Calculate the remaining storage window for each resource separately: free storage divided by current net hourly production. Use the shortest window, then leave room for a late login. Imported resources, a completed upgrade or a temporary production item can change the starting balance and rate.

For example, 6,000,000 free Metal storage at 300,000 Metal per hour provides 20 hours before the threshold. A collection after 12 hours adds 3,600,000 Metal and leaves 2,400,000 free space under those assumptions. Crystal and Deuterium need their own checks. This is a storage calculation, not a safe amount to leave exposed.

Cargo should cover the stock you intend to move, with enough fuel and ordinary fleet slots for the route. More storage prevents production from stopping at the threshold; it does not protect the resources from a raid. Compare a storage upgrade with a shorter collection interval, extra transport capacity and a less concentrated holding location.

sections.title: Compare complete projects at the margin

rows: Additional net production at the actual operating settings
Energy, construction time and resource balance
Extra production after power is supplied
Active limit, energy purchase and fusion fuel
Useful output or fuel savings across affected reactors
Research time, supporting reactors and required utilization
Extra account output from this purchase
Population and tier unlocks, local discounts and displaced research
Astrophysics, colony search, transport, power and collection effort

paragraphs: Do not rank entire technologies by their headline bonus. Compare the next affordable purchase with alternatives that solve the same account goal. A short payback is helpful, but a project can still be wrong when it consumes the Crystal or Deuterium needed for a more urgent unlock.

Additive bonus totals also need a marginal calculation. In an illustrative system where output is base × (1 + bonus), moving the bonus from +100% to +110% changes output from 2.00 × base to 2.10 × base, a 5% final increase. Apply this only to a bonus known to share that additive term; do not merge every OGame bonus into one invented bucket.

sections.title: Keep the income running after disruption
paragraphs: Separate the next upgrade budget from the operating reserve. The reserve should cover the transport, fuel and power assets your collection routine depends on. A large theoretical daily income is little help if missing cargo leaves it parked on several planets.

After a raid or a class change, recheck power, net Deuterium, active crawlers, cargo capacity and the next collection window before resuming the investment queue. Restore the bottleneck that keeps production usable, rather than rebuilding the previous layout automatically.

Review the plan when your available time changes. A more passive setup may be worthwhile even if a fully active expedition model earns more on paper. Compare realistic weeks, including missed logins, rather than choosing between an ideal miner and an ideal expedition account.

checklist: My storage and collection plan fit my actual offline interval.
Crawler comparisons include power and net Deuterium costs.
I evaluated Energy Technology across the reactors that benefit.
My next Lifeform purchase has a specific output benefit and full unlock cost.

guides.title: Expedition play style
guides.summary: Turn a sustainable launch schedule into income, then invest in the bottleneck.
guides.label: Play-style reference
guides.status: Play-style decisions reviewed 9 November 2026. Compare the current universe, class and active bonuses; examples are conditional planning comparisons.
objectives: Build a reliable expedition cycle before investing in its maximum theoretical output.
Choose Lifeform upgrades by the bottleneck they remove.
Track spendable resources, ship finds, fuel and losses separately.

sections.title: Count the launches you will really make
sections.body: This path rewards regular attention. Discoverer is the class to compare first for an expedition-centered account, but use the current class bonuses and your universe’s actual rules. Start with the hours you can relaunch, not the hours a spreadsheet assumes you are awake. Record a normal week including workdays and weekends. Mines remain valuable income while you cannot launch.

callout.title: Do not fund the plan with a lucky screenshot
callout.text: Resources and useful ship finds vary. Black holes, hostile encounters, empty results and delays are part of the operation. Keep a replacement reserve before expanding it.

sections.title: Build the working fleet and schedule
steps: Read the expedition mechanics guide. Confirm Astrophysics, total fleet slots, class, economy speed, relevant bonuses and the current reward bracket before calculating a fleet.
Create one replaceable expedition fleet with sufficient cargo and the appropriate support ships. Keep your core transport and fleetsave capacity separate.
Run a test cycle. Inspect the report and actual returning cargo. Check whether your normal launch time leads to a return you can cover.
Repeat only across the slots you can maintain. Save the last batch’s landing window with extra margin for delays before your planned offline time.
sections.body: An expedition build has two different limits: the reward the mechanics allow and the cargo you can bring home. More cargo can solve a transport limit, but excess cargo does not endlessly raise the reward cap. Likewise, travel-speed improvements help only when shorter travel becomes an extra real cycle or a more reliable schedule.

sections.title: Grow the bottleneck, not everything at once
paragraphs: If reports show insufficient carrying capacity, correct cargo before buying another reward bonus. If fleets sit at home after returning, a speed upgrade may do little for daily launches. If you cannot replace a lost working fleet, build the reserve before increasing launch size. If fuel interrupts the routine, fix Deuterium logistics rather than measuring success only in gross loot.

Once the operation is stable, compare slot-unlocking research, cargo capacity and reward bonuses. Price the entire change, including any extra fleet required for a new slot. Astrophysics that adds capacity is not free income if you cannot afford or relaunch the new fleet.

Keep a daily record of launches, resource returns, usable ship finds, fuel and losses. Treat findable ships separately from resources until you have a real use or conversion plan. A resource-weighting method must match your objective; a large Metal-equivalent total can still leave you short of Crystal for research.

sections.title: Choose Lifeforms around the operation
paragraphs: Compare the building benefits of Humans, Mecha and Rock’tal against your actual split of expedition and mining income. Do not confuse a planet’s chosen species with the technologies selected into its research slots. Once species are discovered, you can assemble research choices across species while keeping the buildings that fit that planet.

Review Enhanced Sensor Technology, Sixth Sense and Telekinetic Tractor Beam for expedition-focused technology choices. Discoverer Enhancement is relevant when you are actually playing Discoverer. Use the current descriptions and compare the next level’s benefit with the cost to unlock and develop it. The Lifeforms guide explains the population and artefact work needed first.

Cargo or speed selections can be sensible logistics choices, but they displace another technology in the same slot. Estimate the production you give up and ask whether the change increases useful capacity, actual cycles or quality of life. A percentage-point change in an additive bonus is not the same percentage change in your final account income.

sections.title: Rebalance when your routine changes

example.title: A useful cargo decision
example.text: If a fleet can already carry its permitted maximum find, another cargo upgrade may reduce the number of cargo ships required per launch. That can lower replacement exposure or simplify logistics. It does not by itself prove higher rewards. Measure the benefit you are actually buying.

sections.body: Review several days or a meaningful batch, not one exceptional result. Change one variable at a time. If work or life reduces your launches, shift investment toward passive production rather than maintaining an old high-attention plan out of habit. The best expedition account is one that you can keep operating without sacrificing fleet safety or sleep.

sections.title: Buy the improvement your reports support

rows: Largest resource finds exceed free cargo
More carrying space or fewer loaded resources
The reward-value threshold or class inputs are wrong
All useful slots are occupied and promptly relaunched
Additional expedition slot and working fleet
Not enough ordinary fleet slots, time or replacement reserve
A faster drive merely creates more idle time
Improve fuel logistics or compare actual dispatch costs
A new fleet composition raises the operating bill
Build reserves and strengthen passive production
Expanding every slot increases simultaneous exposure
The routine is stable with spare cargo
Compare reward research with mine alternatives
The bonus affects ship finds rather than the resource shortage

paragraphs: Make one change, preserve its input assumptions and compare a useful batch. A week of results can reveal a recurring logistics problem, but it cannot establish the true frequency of a rare loss. Keep a long-term record without demanding certainty from a small sample.

sections.title: Price a new slot as a complete operation
paragraphs: A new slot needs more than the research or item that unlocks it. Include the working fleet, any cargo upgrades, fuel stock and enough total mission capacity to keep ordinary transport and fleetsaving available. If the slot is temporary, use only the days when it will actually be active.

Suppose an illustrative permanent-slot project costs 40 million planning units for research and 10 million for its working fleet. If that slot produces an estimated 2 million net per active day, the simple payback is 50 ÷ 2 = 25 active days, not 20. At four active days per week, that is 6.25 weeks before allowing for changing returns or other benefits.

The 2-million figure is an input to test, not an OGame expected return. Estimate it from the extra launches you will really make, with fuel and replacement losses treated consistently. Do not charge the new fleet's entire construction cost against every launch as well as including it in the initial project cost.

sections.title: Value cargo savings and class changes separately
paragraphs: A cargo upgrade can be useful even when it does not increase the permitted reward. If the required carrying space is 120 million, ships carrying 40,000 each require 3,000 units. At 50,000 each, they require 2,400. Removing 600 Large Cargos would reduce base replacement exposure by 7.2 million resource units, provided the remaining fleet still meets the useful expedition-point threshold and support requirements.

That is 25% more cargo per ship and 20% fewer cargo ships for the same capacity. It is not a 25% reward increase. Check the actual launch cost before claiming a specific fuel saving, because consumption depends on the ships, drives, speed, route and modifiers.

For a class switch, calculate the entire account: expedition rewards and slots, mining and crawler effects, research time, transport capacity and the schedule. The October Orion notes changed the non-Discoverer comparison on the test server. Avoid importing the older Collector/General expedition multiplier into a current live recommendation without confirming the universe's behavior.

checklist: My fleet calculation uses the current account and universe inputs.
I retain transport capacity, fuel and a replacement reserve outside expedition fleets.
My next cargo, speed or LF upgrade solves a real measured limit.
I record net returns across a batch and separate ships from spendable resources.

guides.title: Active-fleet play style
guides.summary: Choose targets and logistics before accumulating combat hulls.
guides.label: Play-style reference
guides.status: Play-style decisions reviewed 9 November 2026. Compare the current universe, class and active bonuses; examples are conditional planning comparisons.
objectives: Define the task a combat fleet must perform before buying ships.
Account for fuel, cargo, recovery and an exit plan in a raid decision.
Select class and Lifeform support for the ships and missions you really use.

sections.title: Decide what your fleet is for
paragraphs: An active fleet is an operating expense as well as an asset. Decide whether you want small profitable raids, organized alliance combat, debris collection or another specific activity. Those goals require different speed, cargo and fighting capability. General is the class to compare for combat-focused activity, but class bonuses do not turn an unsuitable fleet into a profitable one.

Begin with a role you can evaluate and a fleet you can afford to replace. Do not copy a fixed battleship-to-fighter ratio from an unrelated account. Enemy composition, technologies, defenses, universe settings and allied participation can change the result. A combat simulator is part of planning, not a license to assume a win.

sections.title: Make the support system reliable
steps: Learn fleetsaving and practise the route with a small fleet. Know where the main fleet will go when you are offline and how you will cover the return.
Prepare enough Deuterium for the intended flight and the next safe move. A successful attack can still strand a fleet if you spend its last fuel.
Provide cargo for the intended resource recovery and appropriate recycling capacity when debris collection is part of the plan. Do not count a debris field as recovered profit before it is collected.
Use research and facilities to unlock the ships and handling capacity required for the chosen role. Do not fund extra combat hulls while basic fuel and transport are missing.

callout.title: Defenses cannot protect an unattended valuable fleet
callout.text: They can change an attacker’s calculation, but a sufficiently valuable target can justify a larger attack. The fleet’s movement and landing plan remain essential.

sections.title: Use a launch decision checklist
paragraphs: Read the most relevant intelligence you can obtain. Check what the report actually reveals and what remains unknown. Simulate with the technologies, ships, defenses and universe settings you can support. If a missing input could change the result, run a conservative case or do not take the fight. The simulation is only as reliable as the information entered.

Calculate expected usable loot and collectable debris, then subtract fuel and expected replacement losses in a consistent resource valuation. Allow for the possibility that the target moves, reinforcements arrive or someone else collects debris. Your original expected outcome is not guaranteed because the fleet has launched.
steps: Confirm the intended target, mission type, chosen fleet, speed and arrival time.
Check that you can monitor the relevant flight and landing window and have a safe post-return plan.
Review current rules governing attacks and allied coordination in your universe. Do not infer permission from another server’s settings.
After dispatch, verify the event list and continue monitoring for material changes. If the situation no longer matches the plan, reassess rather than treating the original simulation as binding.

sections.title: Support the fleet you actually fly
paragraphs: Read the Lifeform technologies that apply to your chosen ship classes, fuel, speed, cargo or combat characteristics. Compare their benefit with normal combat or engine research and with simply buying the missing support ships. A technology for a ship you rarely use can be poor value despite an impressive percentage.

Mecha is a candidate to examine for fleet-oriented buildings, not a compulsory identity. Planet species, selected research and account class are separate layers. You can preserve an economic building setup while selecting a useful technology from another discovered species. Pilot changes on one suitable planet and record the actual bonus before repeating them across the account.
Research that changes speed can change your usual return schedule. Recheck travel times and fleetsave plans after upgrades. A stronger fleet with a return you cannot cover is not a safer fleet.

Check slot positions before assuming two useful technologies compete. Human Cruiser Mk II is in slot 10 and Mecha General Overhaul (Cruiser) is in slot 9, so a cruiser-focused plan can select both. They still compete with the other choices in their respective slots. Use the current Lifeforms tables for effective contributions and unlock costs instead of treating one ship focus as an automatic empire-wide recommendation.

sections.title: Review the operation, including the miss

example.title: A failed raid is still data
example.text: If the target moved and the fleet returned empty, record fuel spent, the observation you missed and whether the flight left other commitments exposed. Do not erase the result from the average. A routine with frequent empty flights can be less profitable than a smaller, better-qualified set of targets.

sections.body: Keep reports and lessons in an appropriate private place. Public guides do not need real coordinates, fleet schedules, names or account screenshots. Review the sequence: intelligence, decision, launch, monitoring, collection and safe return. Improve the weakest step before increasing the fleet’s value. Alliance cooperation details will live in their own section once its mechanics and operating procedures are confirmed.

sections.title: Build a fleet for a repeatable job

headers: Support that belongs in the plan
rows: Enough carrying space, affordable flights and supervised returns
Usable loot after fuel, failed launches and competition
Current timing evidence, suitable speed and a safe return
Correct mission visibility and conservative combat inputs
A tested composition, losses and missile preparation if used
Equal-cost simulator comparisons rather than a fixed ship ratio
Appropriate harvesting capacity, fuel and timing
A realistic collection share, not the whole field by assumption
Agreed roles, rules, attendance and follow-up handling
The actual combined fleets and a plan if participation changes

paragraphs: The same ship can be excellent for one job and an expensive passenger in another. Grow the component that prevents a good operation from working: cargo, harvesting, scouting, speed, combat strength or fuel. Do not treat the largest possible fleet value as the objective by itself.

sections.title: Keep operating liquidity after buying hulls
paragraphs: Reserve Deuterium for the planned operation and the next safe move. Use the dispatch screen with the real composition, route and speed. Fuel reductions, class modifiers and server settings should be reflected in that number; do not subtract a remembered percentage again.

If a moon holds 1,000,000 Deuterium, a planned attack needs 600,000 and a safe post-return departure needs 500,000, the combined plan is 100,000 short. Expected loot is not a reliable substitute for fuel already in the right place. Replenish the moon or change the operation before committing.

Keep replacement and transport resources available as well. A win that leaves the account unable to move its other fleets can be a poor overall decision. Recycle only what you can actually collect, and do not spend predicted debris before the harvest result exists.

sections.title: Test the decision when the target changes
paragraphs: Use at least a normal case and an adverse case. The adverse case should reflect the uncertainty that matters: missing combat research, extra defenders, less loot, incomplete debris recovery or a changed arrival. A simulated victory with one optimistic input is not enough for an expensive launch.

If full debris recovery produces 4 million net but no recovery produces zero, the operation depends on harvesting. Treat recycling capacity and timing as a requirement, not a later convenience. If the target can move the loot and the remaining operation loses resources, decide in advance what evidence would make you recall while recall is still available.

Review empty flights and abandoned plans alongside successful hits. Useful metrics include net resources per supervised hour, fuel spent on misses, permanent ship losses and whether every return was handled safely. These are management choices, not reasons to publish sensitive coordinates or flight schedules.

checklist: My fleet has a named role and a funded fuel/transport/recovery plan.
I understand the limits of the intelligence and simulation behind the decision.
My fleet return is covered by a current fleetsaving and attendance plan.
Lifeform and research choices support the ships I actually use.
