guides.title: Start Orion with a plan for your whole account.
guides.summary: What to build first when Orion is enabled, how to spread IAS levels across planets, and what observed mission cards show about possible rewards at higher levels.
guides.label: Merge preparation
guides.status: Orion preparation reviewed 9 November 2026. Reward examples are selected PTS beta18 mission cards from 28 October 2026, not current live quotes or collected income. Confirm activation and prices in your universe.
objectives: Follow a practical first-build sequence once Orion is active in your universe.
Separate total IAS progression, Lithium throughput, mission completion and reward claims.
Judge possible per-mission reward scale from observed cards while keeping total IAS, scan settings and actual mission levels separate.

sections.title: Confirm the feature before spending
paragraphs: The source review of 9 November 2026 recorded Mars and Nembus as US merge targets for the 9–12 November window. That announcement does not explicitly confirm their Orion activation flag. A universe being newly created or receiving merged accounts does not by itself establish that Orion is enabled. Check the feature in your universe before committing resources.

The official version 13.1.0 notice limits its 6 November Orion activation to universes launching that day. Gameforge’s launch release says a global rollout is planned for 30 November. Neither statement settles the merge targets individually. Open your universe’s technology tree and check that the IAS, Lithium conversion and anomaly interface are available before committing a build budget.

callout.title: Use this guide when Orion is enabled
callout.text: The sequence below is a conditional Orion plan, not a claim that a named target is already active. The live technology tree supplies the exact prerequisites, fields, construction prices and restrictions. A missing feature is a reason to wait, not to rebuild around an assumed release date.

sections.title: What to build first, and why
sections.body: Keep your mines, energy and fleet-safety routine working. Orion adds another use for resources and attention; it does not replace the economy that pays for it. This is a spending order, not a fixed timetable or a requirement to use Dark Matter.
steps: Check the live prerequisites and spare fields on each planet you can practically supply. Build the minimum prerequisite facilities needed to place an IAS there. Do not add expensive facilities solely because an old PTS screenshot had them.

Place IAS level 1 buildings across those usable planets. For a target total, buy the cheapest next scanner level available, rather than pushing one planet far ahead. Equal per-planet exponential prices make a balanced network the least-resource route to that total.

Aim first for a modest total such as IAS 50, then stop to run the loop. Enable a small, affordable Lithium conversion workload and read both the hourly input and output. Check the current storage limit; leave a reserve for claiming the reward as well as finding the mission.

Scan for a manageable mission, inspect its actual level, type, stars, waves, participation rules, duration, requirements and reward claim cost. Use ships or delivery cargo you can afford to commit, and cover the return. A large possible reward is not a completed or claimed reward. Check the claim deadline and actual reward-delivery destination; do not assume the reward can wait until your next login.

Complete the qualifying mission and confirm the Control Center unlock. Buy a low level of a relevant bonus building only after its effect and price make sense for the missions you actually run. A ship-focused building has little immediate value if you keep choosing resource rewards.

Advance through the next useful checkpoints: 100, 150, 200, 250, 300 and 350 total IAS. Recheck affordable missions, Lithium supply and claim costs at each step. Continue beyond a checkpoint only when it supports a mission or bonus you can use.

Buy extra discovery capacity, scan results or deeper bonus-building levels only when the existing limit is regularly stopping profitable play. More slots are not more income if you cannot fund claims or finish missions.

callout.title: Balanced levels optimize access, not everything
callout.text: The cheapest network for a given total IAS is not automatically the best Lithium-throughput layout. Local scanner levels, conversion workload, input availability and current bonuses also matter. First solve the access target; then measure the bottleneck before specializing a planet.

sections.title: Total IAS is the sum across your planets
paragraphs: Use T = L1 + L2 + … + Ln, where each L is one eligible planet’s IAS level. Total IAS supports the selectable anomaly level. It is not the exact level of every result, a reward multiplier by itself, or a building level on one planet. Read the mission card and the live unlock requirement.

For a balanced plan from level zero across n planets, set q = floor(T / n) and r = T − n × q. Build r planets to q + 1 and the other n − r to q. Existing uneven accounts should compare the next available upgrade prices instead of demolishing anything to match an illustration.

The table uses 15 hypothetical, equally priced and usable planets. It is not an account requirement. Amounts are cumulative construction costs from IAS 0, in units of each named resource, calculated with the preserved beta13 cost model. They are not current live quotes and do not include prerequisites.

example.title: Why distribute the levels?
example.text: In the same historical model, total IAS 350 across 15 planets costs 32,992,180 Metal. Across 10 planets at level 35 each, it costs 2,446,262,300 Metal. The total access level is the same; the second plan buys much deeper, more expensive local levels. This comparison isolates construction cost. It does not say the two layouts have equal Lithium output or equal real-world setup costs.

sections.title: Build toward a useful unlock, then complete the mission
sections.body: The public beta13 field research recorded the progression below. Use these as planning checkpoints to confirm in the current Control Center, not guaranteed present-day bonus coefficients. Reaching the total IAS alone did not unlock the building: completing the qualifying mission was the trigger. The actual discovered mission level can differ from the level selected for a scan.

rows: Ship rewards, if those are part of your routine.
Lithium-related rewards; verify its current effect after beta16.
Lower resource input for Lithium conversion in the historical tests.

callout.title: 350 is a progression milestone, not a universal first purchase
callout.text: The historical guide used 350 to reach the final recorded building unlock. That does not prove rushing there has the best payback. A smaller account can stop earlier while it learns mission costs; an established account can advance faster if it can fund and complete the missions. In particular, recheck the Lithium Electrolysis Lab and Anomaly Analysis Center effects in current Techinfo rather than treating this old table as a current bonus specification.

sections.title: Map total IAS to a scan setting and a mission range
paragraphs: Keep three numbers separate: T is total IAS across your planets; S is the anomaly level selected for a scan; M is the level of the discovered mission. Total IAS sets the maximum selectable level, but you can choose a lower scan level. The documented variation of about ±20% is around the selected level S. It maps mission access, not the size of the reward.

Before any undocumented integer rounding, the working range is approximately 0.8 × S ≤ M ≤ 1.2 × S. At the maximum setting, S = T, so this becomes approximately 0.8 × T to 1.2 × T. If you select a lower level, use that selected value instead of your total IAS. The examples below explicitly assume a maximum-level scan; decimal endpoints are arithmetic, not a claim about the game’s rounding rules.

example.title: The reported IAS-693 example fits the level range
example.text: At a maximum-level scan with total IAS 693, the arithmetic range is about 554.4–831.6. The observed mission level 658 lies inside it and is about 5.05% below 693. The mission’s selected scan setting was not visible, so maximum-level scanning is an explicit assumption here, not an observed fact.

callout.title: Do not reverse the percentage the wrong way
callout.text: From a mission level M alone, divide: S is approximately between M / 1.2 and M / 0.8, before unknown game rounding. For M = 658, that is about 548.33–822.5. Applying ±20% directly to 658 gives the wrong inverse. This only brackets total IAS if the scan used the maximum setting S = T; otherwise the total IAS can be higher. Do not infer an exact account total from a mission card. For the separately reported total IAS 693, also require S ≤ 693, narrowing the compatible selected-level interval to about 548.33–693. That still does not identify which setting was used.

sections.title: Observed possible rewards can exceed one billion per mission
paragraphs: The evidence pairs a reported total IAS of 693 with a card-visible level-658 Alien Encounter in PTS beta18. That card displayed approximately 1.415 billion Metal + Crystal + Deuterium in possible rewards for one mission. This supports billion-scale possible rewards at that reported IAS; it does not establish a typical payout or a reward formula.

The five examples below were visually read from mission-summary cards dated 28 October 2026, all on version 13.1.0-beta18 and all PvP combat. Possible Rewards appeared in the mission summary, above separate wave information. The separate Mission Rewards area showed No rewards. These are displayed possible resources per mission, not one wave, an actual claim, net profit or daily income.

The screenshots establish actual mission levels, templates, stars, waves and displayed reward costs. Total IAS 693 is separately reported for the level-658 example only, not visible on its mission card. The other four IAS totals and every selected scan level remain unknown. Every resource amount was marked approximate in the interface, so the sums below are approximate too.

Raw resource units means the arithmetic sum of Metal + Crystal + Deuterium. It is not Metal-equivalent value: one unit of each is simply counted as one. Ships and other non-resource rewards are excluded from this sum. The displayed Reward Costs are shown separately in Lithium units. These rounded interface amounts were not paid or independently verified as the full liability; scan costs, conversion inputs, fuel, delivery costs and losses are not deducted.

For planning at a different IAS total, first map the mission-level range from the scan setting, then compare current cards of the same template, stars, waves and mode. These five unlike cards support a scale comparison, not a line to extrapolate to IAS 500 or 1,000. More IAS opens higher mission levels; it does not assign one payout to every mission in that range.

headers: Possible M + C + D, raw units / mission

example.title: The billion-resource example, with units intact
example.text: At actual mission level 658: ≈841,230,171 Metal + ≈372,945,376 Crystal + ≈201,254,900 Deuterium = ≈1,415,430,447 raw resource units possible for the mission. The displayed reward cost was 55.418 million Lithium. The reward had not been collected. This rounded Lithium display is a separate cost indication, not a subtraction in the same units and not the full cost of running the mission.

callout.title: Observed scale, not an expected return or reward ceiling
callout.text: These five selected cards at actual mission levels 617–772 span roughly 605 million to 1.415 billion possible raw resource units per mission. They differ in template, stars and wave count; class, bonuses and other settings are not fully recorded. This is not a random sample, a confidence interval, an average return, a guaranteed minimum or a maximum obtainable reward. A higher-level card in this set can show less than a lower-level card. Do not fit one global reward curve through them.

sections.title: Turn possible rewards into a measured return
steps: Record the game version, total IAS, selected scan level and actual mission level separately. Keep the mission type, stars, mode, waves, class, bonuses, participation and claim fraction alongside each result. Compare like with like.
Record the total actually claimed across the mission, not one wave copied as a whole-mission total or the possible reward shown before completion. Treat an unknown value as unknown.

For a given IAS band, divide the total actual reward by all attempted comparable missions if you want a return that includes failed attempts. Keep reward per successful full claim as a separate measure. Several observations are more informative than one lucky card.

Observe a full real day or week, including waiting for Lithium, travel and attention. The simplest gross daily return is total actually claimed over that period divided by elapsed days. Keep denominators matched: average per attempt × attempts per day, or average per successful full claim × successful full claims per day. Never multiply an average that already includes failures by successful completions only.

Subtract the resources spent producing the Lithium for scans and claims, plus delivery costs, fuel and unrecovered fleet losses. Use a stated exchange rate if combining Metal, Crystal and Deuterium into one value. Do not treat Lithium as free because it is produced in a building.

Compare the measured extra daily net return with the price of the next IAS upgrades. A rough payback is upgrade cost divided by extra daily net return, in the same value units. If the extra return is zero or negative, that calculation gives no positive payback.

example.title: A large card is an opportunity, not income already earned
example.text: The observed level-658 card offered ≈1.415 billion raw resource units, but its collected-reward area was still empty. Keep that possible amount separate from the amount actually claimed and from the resources needed for its displayed 55.418 million Lithium reward cost, subject to confirmation when claiming. Value Metal, Crystal and Deuterium with an explicit exchange rate before comparing net returns. No daily-income figure can be inferred from this card alone.

sections.title: Patch changes that an old Orion guide can miss
sections.body: The preserved source is guide 0.19.6, dated 11 October 2026, commit 56a951b, describing PTS v13.1.0 beta13. Later official changes take precedence. This list explains specific limits; it is not a complete changelog or a claim that beta17 is the newest release.

rows: IAS construction scaling changed from 1.4 to 1.5; Lithium base production changed to 15.36.
Old cost and production estimates must be version-labelled.
Discard the old unlimited-storage claim; check the current cap.
Explicit Lithium rewards removed; any reward claim can give additional Lithium by chance.
Do not budget guaranteed Lithium from a mission reward.
Earlier ship-yield samples cannot quote present-day returns.

callout.title: No universal Lithium-income calculator
callout.text: The old production example used an inferred ×10 economy factor and lacked fresh post-rebalance validation. It is not used here as a current income prediction. Read live hourly input/output and storage figures instead.

sections.title: What the preserved cost model calculates
paragraphs: For the historical IAS model, the base resource costs are 84 Metal, 42 Crystal and 14 Deuterium. At target level L, the formula is floor(Base × 1.5^(L − 1)) separately for each resource. A current-to-target result sums each next level through the target. The implementation uses exact integer arithmetic with 3/2, not floating-point estimates.

The beta13 official notes increased the scaling factor from 1.4 to 1.5. The preserved calculator follows 1.5, represented exactly as 3/2. Its outputs remain historical projections and require a live-price check before use.

This calculator prices one planet only. A combined account target of 350 means adding the scanner levels on all eligible planets; do not type 350 into a single-planet target field. For a network, calculate each planet separately and add the same resource columns. Prices exclude prerequisites, facilities, transport and opportunity cost.

example.title: Worked historical example: IAS 0 → 2
example.text:
Level 1: 84 Metal + 42 Crystal + 14 Deuterium.
Level 2: 126 Metal + 63 Crystal + 21 Deuterium.
Combined projection: 210 Metal + 105 Crystal + 35 Deuterium.
This verifies the calculation method, not today’s in-game pricing.

sections.title: A final check before the next build
steps: Confirm Orion activation, current prerequisites, construction prices and your usable planets in the current universe.
Keep total IAS, each local IAS level, actual mission level and completed-mission unlocks separate.
Compare one live construction price against the historical model before using its network table or calculator. A mismatch means stop relying on that projection.
Reserve enough Lithium for the scan and the reward claim, and price the ordinary resources used to make it.
Use actual claimed rewards and sustainable completion rates to decide on the next checkpoint. Keep private coordinates, planet names, balances, fleet details and screenshots out of public research.

checklist: Orion is enabled in my universe, and I have checked its current prices and prerequisites.
I have a balanced access target, a Lithium budget and a manageable first mission.
I know that a qualifying completed mission, not total IAS alone, triggers a recorded building unlock.
I keep total IAS, the selected scan level and the actual mission level separate when comparing reward cards.
I distinguish possible mission rewards from actual claims, net return and daily income, and I am not treating selected examples as an average or a guaranteed payout.
My next upgrade is justified by current costs and actual returns, not only a possible reward card.

guides.title: Lifeform population and unlock builds.
guides.summary: Research thresholds, cost-oriented building endpoints and the food and conversion model behind them.
guides.label: Reference
guides.status: Reviewed 9 November 2026. Source-model reference, not a live-account measurement. Official workbook vintage and current implementation caveats are stated below; live Techinfo takes precedence.
objectives: Find a starter or the next useful research milestone.
Compare capacity, food support and actual tier counters.
Price an endpoint with its prerequisites and stated cost scope.

sections.title: What these builds measure
paragraphs: These cost-oriented reference endpoints unlock useful research milestones under the stated equilibrium model. They are not universal optimal builds, a cheapest chronological purchase order, or an instruction to demolish higher levels. Retain existing higher levels and meet all prerequisites. The next useful research slot is usually a better target than all eighteen at once.

All Lifeform buildings use zero ordinary planet fields. There is no ordinary-field advantage between these population packages. Least total resources, least weighted resources, fewest upgrades and fastest completion are different goals. Queue speed, growth time, existing buildings and items can change the best next purchase.

The examples assume no population item or research modifier. Species experience boosts technology bonuses, not these population-building effects. Do not add the old Trader population bonus: it was a bug removed in 2023. Species choice is mainly about local building benefits; researched technologies from discovered species can be selected independently.

callout.title: Capacity, sustainable population and actual population differ
callout.text: Housing is a ceiling. Food determines how much population can be supported indefinitely, while the current counter must still grow to that level. Stored food can bridge a shortage but is not permanent food production. These endpoints deliberately feed slightly less than full housing capacity while still meeting the target. T2 and T3 are chained tier proportions; do not add all tier counters and subtract that sum from housing.

sections.title: Research slot population thresholds
sections.body: Compare each slot against the population of its required tier, not total population. The base table is shared by all species before a Kaelesh Psionic Modulator reduction.
paragraphs: Kaelesh slot requirement = base requirement × (1 − min(0.30, 0.02 × Psionic Modulator level)). Level 11 reduces every threshold by 22%; level 15 reaches the 30% reduction cap. This lowers the requirement, not the actual population counter.

sections.title: Real first-slot prerequisites
paragraphs: Research-building level 1 opens the tree. Some older population-only starter rows understate farm prerequisites; the levels here include those prerequisites. A first slot still needs the actual 200,000 population counter.

For discovery, use a Human pilot with Intergalactic Envoys level 1 and keep it active somewhere while changing other planets. Launch discoveries through Galaxy view DNA icons, not position-16 expedition missions. A species does not need a permanent planet merely to keep its discovered technologies available. Continue discoveries until the species needed for the planned selections are found; not every mission produces a useful result.

sections.title: Humans population milestones
sections.body: Read every building column as a target level, not a purchase sequence. Add the research building and applicable prerequisite chain below. For the all-18 endpoint, additional prerequisites are: Research Centre 5; High Energy Smelting 3; Fusion-Powered Production 2.

sections.title: Rock’tal population milestones
sections.body: Read every building column as a target level, not a purchase sequence. Add the research building and applicable prerequisite chain below. For the all-18 endpoint, additional prerequisites are: Rune Technologium 1; Crystal Refinery 6.

sections.title: Mechas population milestones
sections.body: Read every building column as a target level, not a purchase sequence. Add the research building and applicable prerequisite chain below. For the all-18 endpoint, additional prerequisites are: Robotics Research Centre 1.

sections.title: Kaelesh population milestones
sections.body: Read every building column as a target level, not a purchase sequence. Add the research building and applicable prerequisite chain below. For the all-18 endpoint, additional prerequisites are: Vortex Chamber 5; Bio Modifier 5.

callout.title: Some final margins are very small
callout.text: Human, Mecha and Kaelesh all-18 margins are only about 0.032%, 0.011% and 0.0097%. Verify live counters before treating a tier as secure. The FAQ’s displayed 448 million Kaelesh population is normalized to the unreduced threshold; the actual modelled T3 counter is about 349.474 million with Psionic Modulator 11.

sections.title: Population-package costs
sections.body: Cumulative level 1 → target population-package costs, excluding prerequisite buildings, normal power infrastructure, all technology research and artefacts. MSU = Metal + 1.5 × Crystal + 3 × Deuterium, corresponding to a 3:2:1 trade ratio. These are modelled resource values, not live quotes or universal exchange rates.
paragraphs: The FAQ’s Rock’tal model is about 10.624063 billion MSU with Megalith and Mineral Research Centre discounts. It is not an exact chronological from-zero bill: applying final discounts retrospectively changes historical costs. The undiscounted row is shown for a clear, reproducible scope; real purchase timing determines the discount obtained.

Per-level building resource cost in the workbook is floor(base resource cost × cost factor^(level − 1) × level), separately for each resource. Sum levels 1 through the target, applying the appropriate current discount when each level is actually bought.

The cheaper Kaelesh population package alone does not establish the best long-term mine or expedition returns. Technology levels, local production buildings, research amplification, power and a player’s activity can outweigh this opening cost.

sections.title: Dependencies beyond the starter

rows: Research Centre 5 → High Energy Smelting 3 → Food Silo. Residential Sector 41 + Academy of Sciences 1 → Fusion-Powered Production. Fusion-Powered Production 1 → Skyscraper; level 2 → Biotech Lab. Skyscraper 5 is required for Neuro-Calibration Centre.
Meditation Enclave 41 + Rune Forge 1 → Megalith. Megalith 1 → Crystal Refinery. Crystal Refinery 5 → Oriktorium. Crystal Refinery 6 + Oriktorium 1 → Mineral Research Centre.
Assembly Line 41 → Update Network. Update Network 1 → Microchip Assembly Line. Microchip Assembly Line 1 → Production Assembly Hall. Production Assembly Hall 5 → Quantum Computer Centre.

Vortex Chamber 5 → Antimatter Convector. Sanctuary 42 → Halls of Realisation. Halls of Realisation 1 → Chrysalis Accelerator. Chrysalis Accelerator 1 → Bio Modifier. Bio Modifier 5 → Forum of Transcendence. Chrysalis Accelerator 2 → Psionic Modulator.

paragraphs: The Mecha first-T2 milestone includes Microchip Assembly Line 1 because Production Assembly Hall requires it, correcting the population-only FAQ row. Microchip Assembly Line and Chip Mass Production are different buildings. The Rock’tal first-T2 milestone’s extra population helps meet conversion prerequisites; it is not assumed to be a transcription error.

sections.title: Conversion-building population requirements
sections.body: A conversion building’s population prerequisite is separate from its 1%-per-level conversion effect. The requirement rises as the building is upgraded. L is the target building level.
paragraphs: These are construction population gates, separate from the tier trained and the population tier required by a research slot. Check the building’s current Techinfo before upgrading.

sections.title: Reproduce the population model
paragraphs: Let q = housing level, f = food-building level, s = T2 conversion-building level and t = T3 conversion-building level. H = base housing × housing factor^q × (q + 1) × housing multiplier. C = base consumption × 1.15^q × (q + 1) × consumption multiplier. F = base food × food factor^f × (f + 1) × food multiplier.

Sustainable T1 = H × min(1, F/C). T2 = sustainable T1 × s/100. T3 = T2 × t/100. Compare the appropriate tier with its adjusted slot requirement. Use unrounded values internally; displayed counters are approximate because game rounding can differ. C and F are common-scale model values for the food ratio, not a claim about live hourly display units.
items: Humans: housing multiplier = 1 + 0.015 × Skyscraper; consumption multiplier = 1 − min(0.80, 0.01 × Food Silo); food multiplier = 1 + 0.05 × Biotech Lab.
Rock’tal: these population-package multipliers are all 1. Megalith and Mineral Research Centre affect building costs, not this food/housing ratio.
Mechas: housing multiplier = 1 + 0.02 × Production Assembly Hall; food multiplier = 1 + 0.02 × Microchip Assembly Line; consumption multiplier = 1.
Kaelesh: housing multiplier = 1 + 0.02 × Chrysalis Accelerator; consumption multiplier = 1 − min(0.50, 0.01 × Antimatter Convector); food multiplier = 1.

sections.title: Growth, timing and activation
paragraphs: Finished buildings do not instantly activate a slot. The actual tier counter must reach the requirement and remain there. Official version 9.0.3 made population growth independent of server speed, so an ×8 economy does not imply ×8 population growth. A complete current growth-ETA formula has not been independently verified here.

Human Food Silo reduces upkeep while Skyscraper and Biotech Lab support housing and food. Mechas combine housing and food boosters. Kaelesh combines housing, upkeep and requirement reductions; Cloning Laboratory can be a growth-time option but is not needed for the shown equilibrium endpoint. Rock’tal instead gains cost-reduction options whose purchase timing matters.

sections.title: Unlock tiers without buying unnecessary population
sections.body: There are eighteen research slots arranged in three tiers. Housing and food support the population; conversion buildings make higher-tier population available. For Humans, Academy of Sciences converts toward tier 2 and Neuro-Calibration Centre toward tier 3. For Rock’tal, the analogous progression uses Rune Forge and Oriktorium. Inspect the population tier required by your target slot: a large tier-1 population does not automatically satisfy a tier-2 requirement.
steps: Pick the next useful research slot and write down its displayed population requirement and tier.
Price the missing housing, food, research-building prerequisites and conversion levels as one package.
Build food and housing support, then the required conversion infrastructure. Check actual tier counters rather than total population alone.
Wait for stable population and confirm that the research stays active. A population shortfall can deactivate unlocked technologies.
Buy a useful research level and compare the actual gain before pursuing the next population threshold. Do not rush tier 3 simply because a template shows all eighteen slots.

sections.title: Develop the species buildings in phases
paragraphs: For a mining-oriented Rock’tal pilot, first use Meditation Enclave, Crystal Farm and Rune Technologium to reach the useful early research slots. Then price Magma Forge for metal, Crystal Refinery for crystal and the lifeform Deuterium Synthesiser for deuterium against another ordinary mine level. The lifeform synthesiser is a different building from the normal resource-menu synthesizer.

Before a large development phase, compare the cost savings from Megalith with the cost of buying it. Develop Rune Forge only when a useful tier-2 slot justifies the extra population infrastructure; use the same test for Oriktorium and tier 3. Add Disruption Chamber when the energy benefit or reduced demand solves a measured constraint. This gives a sequence with stop points rather than an unfunded all-buildings shopping list.

An expedition-focused player can still use Rock’tal buildings while selecting expedition technologies discovered from another species. Humans and Mecha deserve comparison when their research-amplifying buildings fit a developed, active account. Species, player class and research selection are not required to match names.

sections.title: Research and reset references
sections.body: Price the desired technology before its population package. Research levels, artefact selections and species switches are separate investments.

Prerequisite buildings, power and technology costs are budgeted separately.

guides.title: Lifeform research: stacking, caps and selections.
guides.summary: How to read the research tables, combine eligible bonuses and distinguish caps from current-version uncertainties.
guides.label: Reference
guides.status: Reviewed 9 November 2026. Source-model reference, not a live-account measurement. Official workbook vintage and current implementation caveats are stated below; live Techinfo takes precedence.
objectives: Find the target and base effect of each technology.
Separate local research levels from account-wide contributions.
Check caps, conditions and source-version limits before investing.

sections.title: Base effects and eligible targets
paragraphs: Every research effect in the four tables contributes account-wide, but only to its named target. Selection and levels are local to each planet. The planet’s inhabiting species is independent of the technology’s origin; the same unlocked technology can be selected on multiple planets. Slots 1–6 are T1.1–T1.6, slots 7–12 are T2.1–T2.6, and slots 13–18 are T3.1–T3.6.

The ship-stat package means structural integrity, shields, attack, cargo capacity and base speed. It does not include fuel consumption. Civilian ships here means Small Cargo, Large Cargo, Colony Ship, Recycler and Espionage Probe, not Pathfinder. Probe cargo still depends on universe settings.

Production percentages act on the relevant production basis, not necessarily on an already-bonused total. Flight-speed, ship-stat and expedition coefficients are not complete final-speed, flight-time or yield equations. Read a research name together with its target: Low-Temperature Drives affects Espionage research, and Rune Shields affects Armour research.

sections.title: How contributions stack
paragraphs: For an ordinary linear effect, the per-planet contribution is base coefficient × research level × (1 + inhabiting-species experience bonus + applicable building bonuses). Add eligible contributions across planets, then apply the relevant effect-category cap. Bonuses inside this multiplier are added, not multiplied independently. The Cloning Lab’s technology amplification applies to Kaelesh technologies.

This expression describes the Lifeform contribution, not the complete final mine, ship, flight or reward calculation. Do not amplify an already-final in-game bonus a second time. Special handling, such as the first level of Intergalactic Envoys, can differ from the ordinary expression.

example.title: A coefficient is not the final production change
example.text: High-Performance Extractors gives 0.06% per level. At level 10 its base contribution is 0.6%; with a combined 10% applicable amplifier it becomes 0.66%, not 10.6%. Two such eligible planets contribute 1.32 percentage points to the relevant production modifier before other system rules.

sections.title: Caps and version limits
sections.body: These are effect-category caps in the referenced definitions, not a separate allowance for every technology. “No cap specified” is not proof that every downstream system is unlimited.

rows: Applies only to the named target; do not treat time reduction as resource savings.
Combine eligible reductions within the applicable calculation.
Ion Crystal Modules does not raise the overload setting.
Slingshot Autopilot refunds fuel on recall; it is not a general flight-fuel reduction.
Psionic Network targets this event probability, not all expedition losses or combat damage.
Raw resource/energy production, ship/defense stats, cargo, phalanx range and class amplification
No cap specified in these definitions
Final-system limits and integer rounding can still matter.
Version conflict: older LF definition 30%; later global limit 90%
See the fuel caveat below; do not substitute either number for an unverified combined formula.

callout.title: Fuel: older Lifeform cap versus later global cap
callout.text: Efficiency Module and Heat Recovery each have a verified base reduction of 0.03% per level. The 2023 workbook and pinned Tracker Lifeform definitions retain a 30% Lifeform cap. The official live version 13.0.0-r8 notice of 29 July 2026 instead states a 90% global fuel-reduction limit. The exact current Lifeform/class/global combination was not independently verified. Do not claim all fuel reduction is capped at 30%, or that each technology independently allows 90%. Check current dispatch fuel and Techinfo.

sections.title: Class enhancements
paragraphs: Rock’tal Collector Enhancement, Mechan General Enhancement and Kaelesh Discoverer Enhancement all occupy slot 18 / T3.6. Each has a base +0.2% per research level to eligible bonuses of the corresponding active class. They do not give an account another class.

A total 50% enhancement means an eligible base perk ×1.5, not an extra 50 percentage points added to every perk. Integer perks have rounding thresholds. The official October 2026 expedition guide gives one extra expedition slot per 50% Discoverer enhancement, amplifying the class’s base +2 slots.

rows: Light Fighter instant Deathstar destruction chance; transport of attacking wreckage to the starting planet; detailed fleet-speed controls; shipyard-acceleration discounts.
Expedition-debris visibility; inactive-player loot; research-acceleration discounts.

sections.title: Effects that need an extra check
items: Intergalactic Envoys unlocks discovery missions at level 1. The official workbook lists a nominal +1% discovery-flight speed per research level; pinned Tracker gives zero speed bonus at level 1, then 1% × level at higher levels. Exact first-level handling and live travel time were not independently verified. It does not improve discovery or artefact odds.

Telekinetic Tractor Beam, Enhanced Sensor Technology, Sixth Sense and Gravitation Sensors increase the quantity of their named expedition find, not the chance of that event. Telekinetic Drive affects expedition travel speed, not holding time.

Psionic Network reduces the probability of the complete-fleet-loss expedition event relatively. It does not reduce pirate/alien battle damage, remove every risk or make fleetsaving on expeditions safe.

Ion Crystal Modules has +0.1% crawler production efficiency and −0.1% crawler energy use per level in the checked definitions. The exact enhanced crawler-production equation remains unverified because the pinned Tracker implementation is internally inconsistent. No final output equation or higher overload setting is inferred.

sections.title: Plan the tier before spending artefacts

example.title: Illustrative comparison
example.text: Imagine one new research level produces an estimated 20,000 additional resources per day across your account and costs 400,000. Its simple payback is 20 days. A second option appears cheaper at 150,000 but requires 500,000 of population infrastructure first: compare 650,000 with its benefit. These figures illustrate total-cost reasoning, not real technology costs.

paragraphs: Artefacts let you select a desired technology rather than rely on a random choice. The official information describes different costs by tier. Before spending, write out your desired selections for the whole tier and compare the total with your inventory. The FAQ warns that changing selections can involve resetting the tier and selecting its technologies again.

The published artefact prices are 200 for a tier-1 selection, 400 for tier 2 and 600 for tier 3. Four deliberate tier-1 selections therefore need 800 artefacts; that is selection currency, not the resources needed to research the chosen technologies. Record the other selections before resetting, because they may also need to be selected again.

Treat a reset as a small migration project: record current selections, check the current interface warnings and costs, and know the desired end state. Do not reset while tired simply because one technology looks better. If a species switch is also involved, evaluate the new building setup and population unlocks before expecting the old bonus to remain active.

sections.title: Choose a build strategy for your actual income
sections.body: These are candidate paths, not an instruction to choose every listed technology. Options in the same slot compete with one another. Preview the slot’s four candidates and their current descriptions before committing artefacts.

rows: High-Performance Extractors: all-resource production; Acoustic Scanning: crystal; High Energy Pump Systems: deuterium
Compare income gained per full upgrade cost. Consider Rock’tal production buildings and Collector Enhancement if Collector is active.
Telekinetic Tractor Beam: ship finds; Enhanced Sensor Technology: resource finds
Add Sixth Sense for resource finds and consider Kaelesh Discoverer Enhancement for an active Discoverer. Value these using actual launches, not an imagined maximum.
Plasma Drive: speed except Deathstars; Efficiency Module: flight fuel reduction
Choose a ship-specific General Overhaul only for ships you use, such as Battlecruisers. Simulate the fleet after updating bonuses.
Cargo Hold Expansion: civilian cargo capacity
Compare fewer ships or trips against the production or expedition technology sacrificed in the same slot. More cargo does not by itself raise the expedition reward cap.

sections.title: Pilot the plan, then roll it out
paragraphs: Try the intended setup on one suitable planet before repeating it everywhere. Record the cost to reach the slot, the research cost and the actual bonus change. If you cannot explain where the improvement appears, investigate before scaling. A copied template may depend on a different class, income mix or activity level.

Compare another level on a mature planet with an early level on a less-developed planet, including prerequisites. Keep core economy, cargo and fleetsave reserves funded. Revisit the plan when your play pattern changes: an expedition-heavy setup deserves a new review if you stop launching regularly. Your account should support the game you actually play, not a schedule you no longer keep.

A species switch preserves previously developed levels for later reuse, but the new species must support and unlock its own selected research. Expect a transition, not an instant replacement of every bonus. Before changing a working setup, record selections, population and account totals. Compare the gain using the production breakdown: a one-percentage-point bonus is not necessarily one percent of an already-bonused total.

sections.title: Evidence and current-game checks
paragraphs: All 72 technology names, targets and base coefficients were checked against Gameforge’s “PTS LF values (current)” workbook sheet and cross-checked with OGame Tracker at commit 052f9dd83ceb18e3188706be4688f0239b8a9c21. The workbook file was last modified on 4 December 2023. Review date: 9 November 2026. These references are not a fresh live-account measurement.

The later official fuel-cap notice takes precedence over a conflicting older definition within its stated scope. Unverified combinations are labelled rather than filled in with a guessed equation. Check the current account’s Techinfo, active bonuses and mission results before a costly change.

guides.title: Compare economic investments.
guides.summary: Mine costs, incremental output, resource bottlenecks and the storage you will actually use.
guides.label: Detailed reference
guides.status: Reviewed 9 November 2026. Published baseline mechanics and calculated scenarios; actual modifiers and game rounding must be checked. PTS evidence is identified separately.
objectives: Compare marginal rather than total production.
Use consistent resource values and full support costs.
Separate payback from the funding date of a useful unlock.

sections.title: Know what each mine does

rows: Construction material; slot bonuses can change the comparison
Research needs can justify prioritizing it despite lower volume
Same level, more output because the planet is colder

callout.title: These are calculated baseline values
callout.text: The table shows formula terms rounded to two decimals, not a promise of the total shown in your resource screen. Compare the screen’s base mine row and modifier rows separately.

paragraphs: Metal funds much of your construction and fleet growth. Crystal is often the limiting material for research and advanced infrastructure. Deuterium is both a construction/research resource and the fuel for operations. Mines provide recurring income while you are offline, but only within energy and storage constraints. An upgrade raises future production; it does not immediately deliver a lump sum of resources.

The standard mine-output terms at full power and ×1 economy are 30 × L × 1.1^L for metal, 20 × L × 1.1^L for crystal, and 10 × L × 1.1^L × (1.44 − 0.004 × Tmax) for deuterium. Tmax is the planet’s maximum temperature. These terms exclude natural base income, slot bonuses, class, Plasma Technology, lifeforms and other modifiers. Multiply resource production by economy speed, then account for your actual bonuses. Do not multiply the power requirement by economy speed.

sections.title: Early production and infrastructure
steps: Open Resources and inspect the Metal Mine, Crystal Mine, Deuterium Synthesizer and Solar Plant. Read the next-level cost, completion time and energy demand.
Use the Solar Plant to support the next mine increase. Check the energy balance after completion; persistent shortages mean the mine is not delivering its intended full output.
Build metal and crystal capacity toward a named early unlock. If crystal is delaying that unlock, increase crystal rather than following a fixed metal-to-crystal level ratio.
Develop deuterium before research and ship fuel become the bottleneck. Do not drain all fuel into a queue once you have ships to move.
Open Facilities for Robotics Factory, Shipyard and Research Lab only as the next unlock requires them. Use the technology tree to see the missing levels.

Before your break, check when each resource will fill storage. Spend on the planned upgrade, improve storage when justified, and establish cargo logistics as ships become available. Return to Resources to verify the result.

sections.title: Measure before you spend
paragraphs: Start on one planet. Write down hourly metal, crystal and deuterium output, available energy, storage space and free fields. Record your class and the universe economy speed next to those numbers. Use the values actually displayed, including active bonuses. A guide written for a different universe cannot supply your production forecast. Refresh the screen after a queue finishes before comparing the result.

Mines need energy, storage limits production, and facilities provide infrastructure rather than direct mine output. These are different problems. An energy shortage is not fixed by another mine, and more storage will not help if you habitually leave a large, profitable stockpile undefended.

sections.title: Name the next constraint
steps: Choose one concrete goal: start the next mine, unlock a colony ship, or fund the next research. Write down the required resources and deadline.

Subtract resources already available and place safe incoming deliveries at their scheduled arrival times. Compare the first time each required resource is available, rather than counting a future shipment as current stock.
Check whether energy, fields, storage or construction time will block the upgrade. Add the necessary supporting work to the plan.
Reserve flight fuel and enough cargo capacity to protect the remaining resources. Spend only the balance.

callout.title: Resource value is contextual
callout.text: A metal-heavy account saving for crystal-heavy research should not blindly choose the biggest metal production increase. Reducing the actual waiting time can matter more than a tidy mine ratio.

sections.title: Compare the complete investment

example.title: Illustrative payback, not game costs
example.text: Upgrade A costs 1,200,000 planning units including its energy support and adds 30,000 units per day: 40 days. Upgrade B costs 800,000 and adds 25,000 per day: 32 days. B has the shorter simple payback. But if B consumes crystal reserved for tomorrow’s colony unlock, delaying it may still be sensible. Neither estimate includes future reinvestment or losses.

paragraphs: For an income upgrade, divide its full cost by the additional daily income it enables. Keep unlike resources separate unless you explicitly choose a conversion ratio for planning. That ratio is an assumption, not a guaranteed trade offer. Include required energy infrastructure and subtract additional operating costs where relevant.

Compare the next level on several planets, not just your largest planet. A small improvement to a developing colony may be easier to fund and leave the account less dependent on one location. Do not call a facility a bad investment simply because it has no direct payback: evaluate the construction delay it removes.

sections.title: Make the offline interval affordable
paragraphs: Current stock plus hourly production multiplied by hours away is an unconstrained forecast. Compare it with each resource’s storage capacity; once storage fills, that mine stops accumulating more. Include timed deliveries, rewards and queued spending separately. If storage fills too soon, an earlier collection, planned spending or a storage upgrade can prevent the lost production. Storage is a buffer, not a security system.

Solar satellites are ships and can be destroyed. Fusion consumes deuterium. Evaluate energy options with their operational risks and net production rather than only their purchase price. Keep a small written recovery plan for a power loss: which mines can be reduced temporarily and what you would rebuild first.

sections.title: Verify the result
sections.body: After completion, check actual output, energy balance and the next storage limit. If the gain differs from your estimate, inspect production settings and bonus expiry before making the same purchase elsewhere. End the session with a named next upgrade and a resource target. Avoid filling queues merely because something is affordable; a deliberate empty queue can be better than an irrelevant expense.

sections.title: Compare the change, not the total
paragraphs: An upgrade earns its return through the difference between the old and new account. For a mine, compare the next level's production with the current level under the same settings. For Plasma or a global Lifeform effect, add the changes across every affected planet. Exclude resource deliveries that would have arrived anyway.

A practical comparison has three lines: the up-front cost; the added daily production; and the new daily operating cost. Include the next required power project, extra fusion fuel and any storage or cargo that is genuinely necessary to use the increase. If the upgrade fits existing spare capacity, do not charge it for infrastructure you already own.

With planning values M = 1, C = 1.5 and D = 3, metal-equivalent value is M + 1.5C + 3D. These weights correspond to a 3:2:1 exchange assumption, not a promised trade. Use the same weights for spending and income. If Deuterium is your operational constraint, test a higher value as well.

Simple payback in days = full incremental cost / additional net daily income. If additional net income is zero or negative, there is no positive simple payback. For a real recovery date, include funding time, construction/research delay and any lost production before completion. Simple payback does not model reinvestment, attacks, bonus expiry or future account growth.

sections.title: A real baseline mine comparison
paragraphs: The classic cost of target level L is floor(base cost × growth factor^(L−1)), separately for each resource. Metal Mine costs start at 60 Metal / 15 Crystal and grow ×1.5; Crystal at 48 Metal / 24 Crystal and ×1.6; Deuterium at 225 Metal / 75 Crystal and ×1.5. Metal and Crystal demand 10 × L × 1.1^L energy; Deuterium demands 20 × L × 1.1^L. Economy speed multiplies output, not these power terms. See the formula reference and maintained building reference.

Example assumptions: mines 30/25/25, ×8 economy, slot 8, Tmax +40°C, full production; no class, Plasma, officer, item, Lifeform or crawler effects. Prerequisites are already owned, and at least 781 energy is spare, so each alternative can run without new power. Costs are classic costs before discounts. Income and energy changes are shown before game display rounding.

Metal narrowly wins this deliberately limited comparison. Crystal can still be the sensible next purchase if it is holding up a useful research, and extra power costs could change the order. A colder planet improves the Deuterium candidate; a different position changes the metal/crystal base. Recalculate after every purchase rather than converting this one example into a permanent mine ratio.

sections.title: Find the actual waiting-time bottleneck
paragraphs: For a named goal with no future deliveries or spending, subtract resources already available from each required resource and divide each remaining deficit by that resource’s reliable net production. The largest result controls the funding time in that simplified model. A positive deficit with no positive income has no finite waiting time. For an actual schedule, add each delivery only when it arrives, subtract planned spending when it occurs, and find the first time all required balances are available together. Subtracting a future cargo immediately can predict a purchase before its resources arrive.

Suppose the remaining deficits are 200,000 M, 150,000 C and 20,000 D, and net production is 20,000/5,000/2,000 per hour. The waits are 10, 30 and 10 hours. More metal does not shorten the 30-hour crystal wait. Any upgrade bought first also consumes resources and takes time, so compare the whole completion date rather than the new production rate alone.

For example, a 100,000-Crystal goal with no current stock and 5,000 Crystal per hour takes 20 hours without deliveries. If 100,000 Crystal is due after 12 hours, the goal becomes fundable at hour 12, not immediately. A delivery due after 30 hours would not shorten the original 20-hour wait. This example assumes no storage constraint, other spending or delivery loss.

sections.title: Value the storage you will actually use
paragraphs: For positive net production, time to full is (capacity − current stock) / hourly production, provided stock is below capacity and no other events intervene. Once a resource reaches its production limit, extending the absence does not keep adding mine income at the old rate. Check each resource separately and include queued costs, incoming cargo and rewards at their actual times. The basic economy reference documents the storage stop.

At 600,000 stock, 1,000,000 capacity and 50,000 per hour, storage fills in eight hours. A twelve-hour absence would lose up to 200,000 production compared with an unconstrained forecast. A larger store is useful if it prevents that recurring loss; an earlier collection can solve the same problem. More storage does not reduce the value an attacker can see sitting on the planet.

All required support and operating costs are included.
I have checked the current resource and technology panels before committing.

guides.title: Plan power around net production.
guides.summary: Solar, satellites and fusion at a common demand, with account-wide research, fuel and recovery costs.
guides.label: Detailed reference
guides.status: Reviewed 9 November 2026. Published baseline mechanics and calculated scenarios; actual modifiers and game rounding must be checked. PTS evidence is identified separately.
objectives: Read the baseline power and fuel formulas.
Compare research with local reactor upgrades.
Measure usable power and net Deuterium rather than surplus alone.

sections.title: Compare three different power sources
paragraphs: Solar Plants are stable, consume fields and have no deuterium operating bill. Solar Satellites use no building fields but can be destroyed; their output depends on the planet’s maximum temperature. Fusion Reactors use fields and deuterium, but their output scales with both reactor level and Energy Technology. Ordinary attacks do not destroy these buildings.

That is fusion’s late-game advantage: large, durable power output from relatively few fields, especially where cold temperatures make satellites weak. It is not automatically the cheapest starting choice. A small account can reasonably prefer solar while it funds colonies and essential research. A mature mining account should compare fusion seriously before committing to another expensive Solar Plant level or a huge satellite fleet.

sections.title: Baseline power and fuel formulas
paragraphs: For the standard unmodified formulas, Solar Plant energy = 20 × L × 1.1^L. Fusion energy = 30 × F × (1.05 + 0.01 × E)^F, where L is Solar Plant level, F is Fusion Reactor level and E is Energy Technology level. Full-output fusion fuel use = 10 × F × 1.1^F deuterium per hour at ×1 economy; multiply the fuel use by economy speed. Energy output itself is not multiplied by economy speed.

Energy Technology raises fusion output without raising this baseline reactor fuel bill. It does not improve Solar Plant or satellite output. Because normal research is account-wide, one Energy Technology upgrade benefits reactors on every planet. Evaluate its combined power gain across the whole account, not only the planet paying for the research.

sections.title: Read the worked comparison
sections.body: Calculated full-output baseline with no class, officer, item or Lifeform bonuses or consumption reductions. Energy is floored and hourly fuel rounded up for this table only. This display convention does not reproduce every server rounding step; use live figures near a threshold.

callout.title: Output comparison, not equal-cost comparison
callout.text: Fusion 20 with Energy Technology 20 supplies 52,041 energy versus 36,207 from Solar Plant 40, using 20 rather than 40 power-building fields. The technology is a separate account-wide investment. These rows do not say the two routes cost the same.

sections.title: Temperature and satellite scale

example.title: Price the next decision, not the whole past
example.text: If you already own Fusion 20 on ten planets, a new Energy Technology level benefits all ten. Compare its cost with ten local reactor upgrades. If you own no reactors, include their construction and the research together. Do not demolish existing solar power simply because a new calculation favors fusion.

paragraphs: At Fusion 20, raising Energy Technology from 16 to 20 increases baseline output from 27,155 to 52,041, about 91.6%, with unchanged baseline fuel consumption. At ×8 economy that reactor consumes about 10,764 deuterium per hour, roughly 258,336 per day before modifiers. Compare that expense with the income enabled by the power, not with your total deuterium stock.

For another perspective, at a maximum temperature of +40°C, the baseline satellite formula floor((Tmax + 140) / 6) gives 30 energy per satellite. Matching the 52,041-energy reactor requires 1,735 satellites. At Tmax −90°C, it gives 8 energy and needs 6,506 satellites. Satellites may still be cheaper upfront; the question is whether you want that much power exposed to destruction.

sections.title: Price useful power at a common demand
paragraphs: Spare energy has no direct sale value. Its benefit is the mine/crawler production it enables, a reactor setting it lets you reduce, a future power purchase it avoids or a reserve against losing temporary supply. Compare alternatives at the same working demand.

For each option, count its additional construction/research cost and its fuel over your planning horizon. Add any replacement allowance and lost production you choose to model, keeping that risk assumption visible. For example, an assumed satellite loss once a year is a scenario, not a measured attack probability. Do not charge existing solar buildings their historical purchase cost again, and do not demolish them merely because new fusion capacity now looks attractive.

At low demand, an affordable Solar Plant level or a manageable satellite batch may preserve resources for colonies and mines. At large demand, field pressure, cold satellites and recurring crawler power make fusion worth comparing. There is no universal mine level at which every account should switch.

sections.title: Research versus one more reactor level
paragraphs: For reactor level F and Energy Technology E, baseline power is 30F(1.05 + 0.01E)^F. Raising E by one changes power by the ratio ((1.06 + 0.01E)/(1.05 + 0.01E))^F. The baseline full-load fuel bill stays unchanged. This explains why the same research becomes more valuable across a large reactor network.

At Fusion 20 / Energy 20, baseline output is 52,041.70 energy. Energy 21 raises it to 61,032.64, a 17.28% increase. By comparison, Fusion 21 / Energy 20 gives 68,304.74, but full-load fuel at ×8 rises from about 10,764.00 to 12,432.42 Deuterium per hour. The local building gives a larger local power gain; research benefits every reactor. Their prices and construction/research times are different, so output alone does not choose the winner.

If ten identical reactors are present, the Energy 20→21 gain is about 89,909 energy across the account, distributed across those ten planets. It cannot be transferred between planets. A planet without a reactor gains no fusion power. Use each local demand to decide how much of the gain is useful.

sections.title: Turn power into a net-resource comparison
paragraphs: Record total energy balance and final net Deuterium under the old settings. Then compare the proposed workload with the same mine levels and active bonuses. Fusion fuel scales with economy speed; a universe's ship-fuel reduction must not be borrowed as a reactor discount. Apply only bonuses that actually affect the power or fuel line concerned.

An illustrative crawler change adds 9,600 M, 5,760 C and 2,880 D per hour, but needs another 4,000 D per hour of fusion fuel. The retained change is +9,600 M, +5,760 C and −1,120 D. At M1/C1.5/D3 that is +14,880 metal-equivalent per hour, or 357,120 per day. If the incremental power investment costs 10,000,000 in those same units, its simple payback is about 28.00 days. A positive total value can coexist with a worsening fuel shortage; check both the valuation and the actual Deuterium reserve.

sections.title: Switch in a controlled sequence
steps: Record current energy demand, normal net deuterium income and the next mine/crawler demand. Set a fuel reserve you will not consume.
Check the live prerequisites: Fusion requires Deuterium Synthesizer 5 and Energy Technology 3. Price the intended reactor and research levels.
Build enough new capacity before reducing existing supply. Keep mines powered during the transition.
Adjust fusion operation only as needed and verify the resource screen. The table models full output, not every partial-output setting.
Check net production after bonus expiries and after a satellite loss. Revisit the next Energy Technology level across all reactors.

For an established reactor network, test whether the new Energy Technology level lets you lower reactor operation while meeting the same demand. Compare the resulting net deuterium on every planet; spare energy is not the only benefit.

callout.title: Read total energy, not just the satellite row
callout.text: Bonuses can appear separately from base satellite output. When checking a safe proposed change, compare the total energy balance and all affected bonus rows. Do not invent an extra slot-15 penalty or assume the satellite base row already includes every bonus.

sections.title: Leave a workable recovery setting
paragraphs: Check the account after an energy item expires, a relevant officer expires, class changes, or satellites are lost. A small positive surplus supported by a temporary bonus is not durable capacity. If power becomes short, compare reducing crawler overload or a noncritical mine while restoring supply; do not assume buying more mine levels solves the deficit. Keep a reserve for flight fuel and the resources needed to rebuild the chosen power source.

A higher Energy Technology level may permit a lower reactor setting while preserving full production. Verify the actual available settings and net fuel change in Resources. This guide does not assume that a continuous optimization formula exactly reproduces current slider and rounding behavior.

sections.title: The decision rule
sections.body: Prefer fusion when durable power and field efficiency solve a real constraint, the shared research investment is affordable, and net income remains attractive after fuel. Prefer or retain solar when it meets your present demand cheaply, or when the fusion investment would delay more valuable growth. A mixed supply is valid: existing solar can reduce reactor workload while fusion provides the scalable backbone.

objectives: Separate capacity from position access.

sections.title: Decide what the colony is for
paragraphs: A new planet is an investment with several costs: the research that opens capacity, the colony ship, the flight, startup resources and the time spent developing it. Name the purpose first. It could be additional production, a shorter supply route, a deployment partner or access to another area. A good location for one purpose can be poor for another.

Do not copy a coordinate pattern without considering your fleet speed and login schedule. A distant colony can make deliveries inconvenient; a tightly clustered account may be convenient but offer fewer operating areas. Neither layout is universally correct.

sections.title: Check capacity and prerequisites
paragraphs: Use the current Astrophysics panel and technology tree to confirm that another planet is allowed and that the intended position can be colonized. The colony ship requires Shipyard 4 and Impulse Drive 3. The October 2026 administrator guide lists its cost as 10,000 metal, 20,000 crystal and 10,000 deuterium. Include the missing prerequisites and flight fuel in your own budget.

Do not interpret an empty slot as proof that your account can settle it. Check capacity again after any other colonization mission resolves. This guide deliberately does not prescribe a maximum planet count or a universal class bonus: the live interface is the final check.

sections.title: Compare candidate locations
steps: Make a shortlist of empty positions in areas that fit the colony’s role. Note supply distance and useful nearby planets or moons.
Check the surrounding activity. Look for active neighbors and whether your proposed logistics would be comfortable to operate, not merely possible.
Compare the position’s production and temperature implications using current game information. Do not assume proximity to the sun improves every energy source.
Estimate the first supply shipment and its timing. Keep your main account’s next essential upgrade and fleetsave fuel funded.
Recheck the destination immediately before launching the colonization mission. Record when you will be available to inspect the result.

sections.body: The October 2026 colonisation guide identifies these broad position differences. Planet temperature affects solar satellites and deuterium production, not Solar Plant output. Check the generated planet and your universe field bonus rather than assuming the best possible roll.

sections.title: Apply field bonuses in the right place

example.title: A practical slot choice
example.text: For a metal-focused general mining planet, slot 8 offers +35% base metal and a 156–252 base-field range. Slot 1 offers +40% crystal but only 96–172 base fields and much warmer temperatures. Neither bonus describes total account income. Choose according to the resource you need, your field plan, and the energy system you can support.

paragraphs: Base fields derive from planet diameter squared: (diameter / 1,000)^2. Discoverer’s 10% and the Researchers alliance class’s 5% colonization bonuses affect diameter, not fields directly. The 2026 official example turns a 15,000-km, 225-field base planet into 297 fields with both bonuses. Universe extra fields are then added separately. Do not apply a 15% field increase instead.

Lifeform buildings and field items can alter the usable result after settlement; do not treat them as guaranteed base colonization size. The Lifeforms FAQ specifically warns that leaving Kaelesh removes Bio Modifier bonus fields. Reserve room for the infrastructure your plan needs rather than accepting a tight colony only because a temporary setup makes it appear roomy.

Position bonuses increase the mine-production base used by subsequent production bonuses. Do not simply add the position percentage to all other percentage bonuses. For example, unmodified Metal production of 1,000 becomes a slot-8 base of 1,350. A separate 10% mine-production bonus then contributes 135 rather than 100. This isolates the position interaction; a full account calculation must still apply the other bonuses correctly.

sections.title: Inspect before heavily investing

example.title: Illustrative expansion budget
example.text: Suppose research and prerequisites need 700,000 resource units, the ship and travel budget need 50,000, and initial development needs 250,000. Your expansion costs 1,000,000 in this planning example, not merely 50,000. If you have only 800,000 available after fuel reserves, postpone optional development or save more before committing.

paragraphs: The generated planet must be evaluated after arrival. Review its fields, temperature and how it serves the intended role. Set a reasonable acceptance criterion before launching, so you do not endlessly reroll looking for a mythical perfect planet. If it does not meet your needs, pause major spending and compare alternatives. Abandonment is a separate, consequential decision; check its warnings and all assets first.

Ships accompanying colonization are not automatically a permanent local fleet. The administrator guide notes that accompanying ships return after delivering resources. If you need cargo ships stationed there, arrange a separate deployment and verify the mission type.

sections.title: Develop in stages and connect the route
paragraphs: First establish usable production and the energy to support it. Then add only the facilities required by the colony’s next job. Send startup resources in manageable waves rather than leaving the entire future build budget on an undeveloped planet. Do not neglect the supplier while funding the new world.

Treat the colony as operational when it can contribute resources, receive supplies and participate in your safety plan without constant emergency fixes. Test a small transfer, check available cargo and note its next storage deadline. Review the colony after a few sessions: is it reducing a bottleneck, or have you created a location that continually consumes attention without meeting its intended purpose?

sections.title: Capacity and location are separate gates
paragraphs: The research-only baseline is one homeworld plus floor((Astrophysics + 1)/2) colonies. Astrophysics 1 opens the first colony, then each odd level opens another. Positions 4–12 are available at level 1; 3 and 13 at level 4; 2 and 14 at level 6; 1 and 15 at level 8. An empty position still requires both an available colony slot and sufficient Astrophysics. Additional account entitlements, if present, are outside this baseline; use the actual capacity shown before launch. See Colonization.

A Colony Ship requires Shipyard 4 and Impulse Drive 3 and costs 10,000 Metal, 20,000 Crystal and 10,000 Deuterium before any applicable changes. Accompanying ships can deliver resources but return rather than becoming a stationed local fleet. Include flight fuel and a separate deployment when establishing local cargo capacity. See the October 2026 administrator guide.

sections.title: Position and temperature reference
paragraphs: Slot 15 has no flat Deuterium percentage bonus. Its advantage comes from the temperature term 1.44 − 0.004Tmax. At Tmax +50°C that term is 1.24; at −110°C it is 1.88. At equal mine levels and other relevant bonuses, the colder example produces about 51.61% more gross Deuterium. Within slot 15, −130°C versus −90°C changes the term from 1.80 to 1.96, about 8.89% more. Colder does not make Solar Plants or Fusion Reactors less productive.
sections.body: Published unmodified colony ranges from the official 2021 colonization reference; the October 2026 guide confirms the production bonuses. Fields exclude universe, class, item and lifeform adjustments. Temperature ranges below describe possible maximum-temperature values used for production calculations. A range is not a guaranteed roll.

sections.title: Slot 8 versus slot 15: a useful comparison
paragraphs: Consider only mine-derived output from equal Metal 30 and Deuterium 25 mines at ×8 economy, with no bonuses except position, and compare slot 8 at Tmax +50°C with slot 15 at −110°C. This comparison excludes natural base income. The slot-8 metal bonus is worth about 43,972.49 M/hour. The colder slot-15 synthesizer gains about 13,868.42 D/hour. In this stripped-down comparison, the mine-income break-even value is about 3.17 Metal per Deuterium.

This is not a universal ranking. Different metal/deuterium levels, Plasma and Lifeform bonuses, actual temperatures and resource values change it. At 3M per D, the slot-8 metal gain is slightly more valuable in this example; at 3.5M per D, the slot-15 Deuterium gain is more valuable before power and field costs. If both planets use the same fusion setup at the same workload, their baseline reactor burn is the same. If one needs additional fuel or replacement satellites, compare the resulting net output instead.

The best slot can still be a poor operational location. Include collection distance, deployment partners, available time and the surroundings. An ideal paper return that requires a supply schedule you cannot maintain is not a reliable return.

sections.title: Fields are a long-term budget
paragraphs: Base fields are derived from diameter, then integer rounding applies. In the official unenhanced example, a 15,000-km planet has 225 base fields. Discoverer's 10% and Researchers' 5% colonization diameter bonuses combine to 17,250 km; floor(17.25²) gives 297 fields. This is not merely 15% more fields. Universe extra fields are added separately. Do not recover an exact original diameter by taking the square root of a rounded field count.

Budget ordinary building levels, not just mines. Mines 40/35/37 use 112 levels of space; Fusion 22 and retained Solar Plant 20 bring that to 154 before robotics, shipyard, laboratories, storage and other facilities. Reserve practical headroom for the next development stage and use the current field display for the final result. Temporary field effects should not be the only reason a permanently cramped colony looks adequate. The Lifeform reference covers species changes and loss of bonus fields.

sections.title: Price expansion as a project
paragraphs: Count the remaining Astrophysics levels, missing prerequisites, colony ship, travel, startup mines, power, logistics and any intended Lifeform unlocks. Compare that marginal project with improving an existing planet. Do not charge the whole historical account's research to the new colony, but do include both levels when the next planet requires an even-plus-odd pair.

A new planet can benefit from existing global Lifeform technologies and may later add global bonuses of its own. That can improve expansion economics, but only after the necessary local setup and selected technologies are funded. Use a development schedule rather than crediting a mature colony's full income on its first day. Decide a reasonable field/temperature acceptance range before sending repeated colony ships; perfect-roll hunting has ship, time and opportunity costs too.

guides.title: Choose research by its actual benefit.
guides.summary: Astrophysics thresholds and prices, Plasma returns, and eligible laboratory networks.
guides.label: Detailed reference
guides.status: Reviewed 9 November 2026. Published baseline mechanics and calculated scenarios; actual modifiers and game rounding must be checked. PTS evidence is identified separately.
objectives: Find the next capacity threshold.
Compare account-wide production with local investment.
Calculate eligible labs and avoid double-counting research speed.

sections.title: Start with a capability
paragraphs: Pick one result you will actually use: a colony ship, additional fleet capacity, a particular ship, or a production improvement. Research levels are means to those results. A long technology list can tempt you to buy one of everything without ever completing a useful chain.

Open the target’s technology tree and write down every unmet prerequisite. Include building levels as well as research levels. Then order them so each requirement becomes available before you need it. Keep this plan short enough to finish; a list of every late-game technology is not a near-term plan.

sections.title: Classify the benefit
sections.body: Classic research applies across the account. Lifeform technology levels are developed separately on planets, but their applicable active bonuses can contribute across the account. A Research Lab enables technologies and influences research duration. The classic system runs one normal research at a time; a queue schedules work rather than creating parallel classic research. Check current restrictions around laboratory upgrades before starting a long technology.
