callout.title: Unused capacity earns nothing
callout.text: An extra slot helps only if you can fund and manage the additional mission. Research should match your real activity rather than an idealized day with unlimited time.

sections.title: Research costs and prerequisites
steps: Write the target, its prerequisites and the resources needed for each missing step. Use current costs from your account.
Estimate when the slowest resource will be ready. Account for planned spending elsewhere before promising a start time.
Check the lab requirement and displayed duration on the planet where you will start. Compare a lab upgrade only if its total delay and cost are justified.
Schedule any lab work before the long research begins, after checking the current queue restrictions.
Reserve resources for using the unlock. A newly available ship is not helpful if no budget remains to build it or fuel it.

sections.title: Buy time deliberately

example.title: Illustrative schedule comparison
example.text: A technology takes 20 hours now. Preparing a better lab takes 8 hours and reduces that research to 14 hours. For this single goal, 8 + 14 = 22 hours is slower than starting now. If several future researches benefit, the lab may still be worthwhile. Include resource waiting time before deciding.

paragraphs: An expensive lab investment may make sense when you have a sustained research program. It may be wasteful when one affordable unlock is the only immediate objective. Compare the completion date of the entire plan, including the time to fund and construct the lab, rather than only the shorter research timer.

Later, Intergalactic Research Network can combine eligible laboratories; do not assume every lab you own contributes automatically. Read its current description and the technology’s lab requirement before distributing upgrades. The right question is which additional lab actually shortens the research you intend to run.

sections.title: Test the unlocked capability
paragraphs: When research finishes, confirm that the intended action is now available. Recalculate relevant fleet times after drive research; an old fleetsave timetable may no longer fit. If you bought mission capacity, try the additional mission during a session you can supervise. If you expected a production gain, compare the resource screen before and after under the same settings.

Record what the upgrade changed and choose the next bottleneck. Do not immediately buy another level by habit. A useful research plan is revised as the account gains colonies, changes play style or loses the time needed to use an active fleet.

sections.title: The recurring benefits worth comparing
paragraphs: These are the classic baseline effects, before applicable class, officer, item and Lifeform changes. Source: staff research reference and maintained research reference. Fleet-specific drive thresholds and combat research belong with the fleet reference.

rows: Additional colonies on odd levels; expedition capacity at square-number thresholds
Price the remaining research plus a usable colony or an expedition operation you will actually run.
Each level adds 1% Metal, 0.66% Crystal and 0.33% Deuterium on the applicable mine bases
Add the benefit across the account and compare with local mines or Lifeform upgrades.
Changes the Fusion Reactor power formula
Compare useful power and fuel settings across all reactors.
One additional normal fleet slot per level
Useful when mission capacity, rather than ships/fuel/attention, is the real limit.
+5% of base ship cargo per level
Compare extra usable capacity with more cargo ships; do not confuse it with Hyperspace Drive.
Adds another eligible laboratory per level
Useful only while another qualifying lab contributes to the intended research.

sections.title: Astrophysics: buy the next threshold
paragraphs: The formulas are 1 + floor((A+1)/2) total planets and floor(sqrt(A)) base expedition slots. Additional class, item or other account entitlements are separate. Expedition fleets still consume normal fleet capacity, so an expedition slot alone does not guarantee another launch.

Classic target-level costs use bases 4,000 M / 8,000 C / 4,000 D, factor 1.75, with each component rounded to the nearest 100. Sum each remaining level separately, then apply only validated applicable cost reductions. The Astrophysics reference gives this rounding explicitly.

For Astrophysics 17→19, level 18 costs 54,163,500 M / 108,327,000 C / 54,163,500 D. Level 19 costs 94,786,100 M / 189,572,300 C / 94,786,100 D. Total: 148,949,600 M / 297,899,300 C / 148,949,600 D before reductions. This buys the next research-only planet capacity, not a developed planet. Crystal is not exactly twice the already-rounded Metal total because each component is rounded independently.

sections.title: Plasma: the percentage is of the base
paragraphs: Use the applicable mine base, including the appropriate position/economy treatment, rather than multiplying the final total income by the advertised percentage. Additional modifier interactions need their own model; the resource screen is the check for a real account.

Suppose the relevant aggregate hourly bases are 1,000,000 M, 500,000 C and 300,000 D. One Plasma level adds 10,000 M, 3,300 C and 990 D per hour in this unmodified example. At M1/C1.5/D3, the gain is 430,080 metal-equivalent per day.

Classic Plasma level 15 costs 32,768,000 M, 65,536,000 C and 16,384,000 D before reductions. At those weights its cost is 180,224,000 and simple payback about 419.05 days. This is deliberately an illustration of the calculation, not a recommendation for level 15. More planets or higher mines improve the return; a cheaper local upgrade can still win now. If Plasma is not yet unlocked, include the missing prerequisites. The classic prerequisites are Research Lab 4, Energy 8, Laser 10 and Ion 5.

sections.title: Laboratories and IRN: eligibility matters
paragraphs: IRN level N can combine the starting laboratory with up to N additional eligible laboratories. Each contributing lab must meet the minimum lab requirement for the technology being researched. It does not divide one research into parallel independent completions, and it does not let an insufficient starting lab ignore the technology tree.

With laboratories 12, 10 and 8 and IRN 2, a technology requiring Lab 8 can use an effective level of 30. A technology requiring Lab 10 can use only 22. Raising IRN again does not help either example if there is no further eligible lab. Conversely, bringing a nearby lab across an eligibility threshold may contribute its whole level to the network, not just the one new level.

Before modifiers, research time in hours is (Metal cost + Crystal cost) / [1,000 × (1 + effective lab level) × total research speed]. Deuterium is part of the resource price but not this baseline time numerator. For an unchanged research and other factors, increasing effective lab 22→30 changes the timer by 23/31, about 25.81% shorter.

Use the universe's total advertised research multiplier. A server listed as ×10 economy and ×20 research means ×20 in this equation, not ×200. Class, officer, Lifeform and other time modifiers require the actual applicable calculation; compare the final displayed duration before starting. See the October 2026 settings explanation.

sections.title: Time saved is valuable only when the program uses it
paragraphs: Compare completion dates including funding, laboratory construction and any queue restrictions. Eight hours of lab preparation followed by a fourteen-hour technology completes in twenty-two hours, later than starting its present twenty-hour timer immediately. The lab may still pay off over a longer research program.

For expansion, count the even level that lies between today's odd Astrophysics level and the next colony. For an extra expedition slot, check the square-number threshold and whether normal fleet slots, ships and your schedule can use it. For drive upgrades, recheck future launch timings and fuel rather than assuming your old fleetsave settings still fit.

guides.title: Compare crawler capacity and overload.
guides.summary: Working limits, overload energy, production ceilings and net-resource comparisons.
guides.label: Detailed reference
guides.status: Reviewed 9 November 2026. Published baseline mechanics and calculated scenarios; actual modifiers and game rounding must be checked. PTS evidence is identified separately.
objectives: Separate owned units, allowed working count and realized bonus.
Compare marginal overload output with power cost.
Keep baseline arithmetic separate from Lifeform interactions.

sections.title: Understand what you are buying
paragraphs: Crawlers are stationary production support. They cannot accompany a fleetsave, so budget them as vulnerable local infrastructure rather than mobile fleet. The official class FAQ lists Collector as required for construction, with Shipyard 5, Combustion Drive 4, Armour Technology 4 and Laser Technology 4. The base unit cost is 2,000 metal, 2,000 crystal and 1,000 deuterium. Confirm the current technology tree before starting a large queue.

Start with a planet that already has meaningful mine output and reliable power. A crawler bonus on weak mines is small, while its energy requirement still needs funding. Build in batches so you can verify the displayed gain before repeating the purchase across the account.

sections.title: Calculate the working limit
paragraphs: The standard active-count limit is 8 × (Metal Mine level + Crystal Mine level + Deuterium Synthesizer level). Before Lifeform class enhancement, a Collector with an active Geologist has 10% more working capacity. Rock’tal Collector Enhancement can increase that capacity bonus; read the allowed working count in your account. This is not a multiplier from economy speed. Collector’s 50% crawler-output improvement is also not a 50% increase in the number that can work.

Keep three quantities distinct: crawlers owned, crawlers allowed to work, and the production bonus actually realized. A separate 50% crawler-production cap is documented in the official 22 July 2026 PTS 13.0.0-r5 changelog. That is test-server patch evidence, not a fresh measurement of every live universe; confirm the current bonus row in your account. More working capacity does not guarantee more income once that bonus ceiling is reached. Lifeform changes can make the ceiling relevant earlier; inspect the current bonus row rather than blindly filling the count limit.

sections.title: Stop before extra spending stops helping
paragraphs: Without lifeform modifiers, a Collector at 150% workload gains 0.045% per active crawler before the cap. Thus 1,111 yields 49.995%; 1,112 reaches the 50% ceiling if the mine-based limit permits it. This is an arithmetic illustration, not a universal recommended fleet size. Enhanced efficiency, operating settings and your working limit change the useful number.

If raising the workload or building another batch does not raise the crawler production row, stop and check the cap. Do not assume a production enhancement is broken merely because a capped output remains unchanged. If the higher workload only draws more power, reduce it to the lowest setting that preserves the desired output.

sections.title: Measure the marginal return
paragraphs: In the worked 640-crawler example, moving a Collector from 100% to 150% workload adds 9.6 percentage points of baseline crawler production and 32,000 energy demand. It does not add 50% to the entire planet’s total income. If your relevant mine base were 100,000 metal/hour, the uncapped extra crawler metal would be 9,600/hour before other applicable effects. Repeat for crystal and deuterium, then subtract any extra fusion fuel.

Price the extra energy infrastructure as part of the crawler investment. If you use satellites, include replacement exposure in the decision. If you use fusion, compare a shared Energy Technology upgrade with local reactor levels. There is no reason to overcharge simply because the slider allows it.

sections.title: Add crawlers in verified batches
steps: Read mine levels, working limit, current crawler count, energy balance and production bonus on one planet.
Check that the next batch fits the active limit and still produces a useful gain below the bonus cap.
Fund the energy supply and reserve replacement resources before starting the batch.
Compare the resource screen at 100% and at the intended Collector workload. Record net deuterium, not just gross mine output.
Recheck after mine upgrades, class changes, Geologist expiry and lifeform changes. Then repeat only where the result is worthwhile.

sections.title: Three limits, three separate questions
paragraphs: Crawlers are stationary ships that support local mining. Collector is required to build them under the standard class rules; another class can operate crawlers already owned, with its applicable non-Collector effects. The classic unit costs 2,000 M, 2,000 C and 1,000 D and requires Shipyard 5, Combustion Drive 4, Armour 4 and Laser 4.

Baseline working capacity is 8 × (Metal Mine + Crystal Mine + Deuterium Synthesizer levels). Collector with an active Geologist has 10% more before Lifeform class enhancement. The class's 50% output improvement is a different effect; it does not mean 50% more units may work. See the class FAQ.
items: How many are allowed to contribute under the mine-based working limit?
How much of their potential production survives the production ceiling and power constraints?

sections.title: Work through one planet
sections.body: Example: mines 30/25/25 total 80 levels. The base active limit is 640; with Collector and Geologist it is 704. The table uses the baseline bonus of 0.02% per crawler, Collector’s ×1.5 output, and no lifeform effects. All rows assume sufficient energy and stay below the 50% bonus ceiling.

callout.title: 150% workload is not 150% energy
callout.text: The class FAQ states that each 10-point workload increase above 100% costs 20% more energy. At 150% workload, a baseline 50-energy crawler needs 100 energy. Lifeform reductions must be applied separately.

sections.title: Overload buys output at a worse marginal power rate
paragraphs: The no-Lifeform baseline is 0.02% of the relevant mine base per working crawler at 100%, multiplied by 1.5 for Collector. At Collector 150%, one crawler contributes 0.045% before the production ceiling. It does not add 0.045% to the final already-boosted planet total.

The overload increments add 10% of the 100%-setting output for another 20% of its baseline energy. At 150%, output is 1.5 times the 100% result while power is twice as high. That does not make overload automatically bad: spare or efficient power can justify it. It does mean a power-constrained planet should compare its net return, not simply select the largest number.

headers: Bonus per active crawler before cap

sections.title: The production ceiling can arrive before the count limit
paragraphs: The official July 22, 2026 PTS r5 changelog explicitly records restoring a 50% mine-production cap. That source is PTS evidence, not a new measurement on every live universe. Use the current Resources bonus and energy rows when deciding how many units or what workload is useful.

With no Lifeform effects, Collector at 150% gives 1,111 × 0.045% = 49.995%; the 1,112th crawler would cross a 50% ceiling if the count limit permits it. A UI rounded to 50.00% can conceal that small difference, so use actual output as well as the printed percentage. Class enhancement, Ion Crystal Modules and other relevant effects change the useful count; do not apply this number as a universal target.

If the production row stops increasing while energy demand rises, a higher workload is buying no additional mine income. Use the lowest available setting that retains the desired output. Do not assume an efficiency technology is useless merely because production is capped: an independent energy reduction can still matter. Exact Lifeform stacking is covered separately; the baseline table here deliberately excludes it.

sections.title: Count the retained resources
paragraphs: For 640 Collector crawlers, 100→150% adds 9.6 percentage points of the relevant mine base and 32,000 energy demand. With bases of 100,000 M, 60,000 C and 30,000 D per hour, the uncapped extra gross production is 9,600 M, 5,760 C and 2,880 D per hour.

Now price the power that actually supplies those 32,000 units. Additional fusion fuel reduces net Deuterium; satellite supply adds destruction and replacement exposure; a shared Energy Technology upgrade may help several planets. The linked power example shows how positive metal-equivalent income can still worsen the Deuterium fuel balance. If power is short, compare the whole planet before and after, because reduced mine production can outweigh the crawler gain.

Recheck after a mine upgrade, class change, Geologist expiry, energy bonus expiry or a Lifeform change. Do not copy one planet's working count and workload to every colony without comparing its mines, power and actual return.

guides.navTitle: Fleetsaving: route visibility and failure modes
guides.title: Fleetsaving: route visibility and failure modes
guides.summary: A practical reference for choosing a route and handling its return.
guides.label: Detailed reference
guides.status: Evidence reviewed 9 November 2026. Historical formulas and unresolved live-version boundaries are labeled.
objectives: A practical reference for choosing a route and handling its return.

sections.title: Protect the return, not only the departure
paragraphs: Fleetsaving means moving ships and movable resources off a location during your absence. The dangerous moment is often the landing: another player may arrange an attack to arrive immediately afterward. Defenses can discourage a casual raid but do not make a valuable fleet safe.

Decide when you can genuinely be online before choosing a route. Use the game’s arrival display and server clock, not an estimate from yesterday. Research, ship composition and speed settings can change the duration. Leave time to reconnect, inspect events and act; an alarm at the landing second is too late.

sections.title: Choose a method you understand
sections.body: Without a moon, deployment between your own planets is a useful route to understand. Its outbound movement appears on a phalanx scan of the destination planet, not the origin. A recalled Deployment is absent from phalanx, although observations made before recall can help an opponent estimate its return. Deployment to an owned moon has no directly scannable destination. With two suitable moons, moon-to-moon Deployment avoids direct phalanx scans at both endpoints, but moon destruction, predictable habits and an unattended arrival remain risks.

rows: Practice deployment and recall with a small fleet
Outbound visible at destination; recall timing may be inferred
Get an alliance review of available routes
Do not assume any long mission is safe

callout.title: Transport is not deployment
callout.text: Transport unloads and returns. Deployment stations the ships at the destination unless recalled. Verify the mission name and both location types, not just the coordinates.

sections.title: Run the departure checklist
steps: Gather the ships you intend to protect. Check outstanding returns and shipyard completions that could leave ships behind after departure.
Select the destination and confirm whether each end is a planet or moon. Pick deployment only when that is your intended method.
Set speed and read the resulting arrival time. For a recalled save, first practice and inspect the return timer with a small, expendable fleet.
Load resources within capacity, accounting for flight fuel. Make sure the destination or return location will have what you need for the next launch.
Send, then reopen the event list. Confirm the mission exists with the expected ships, cargo and time. A clicked button is not proof of launch.

sections.title: Plan around real life
sections.body: Use two reminders if helpful: one before you need to log in and one before the critical event. An unreliable connection is a reason for more margin, not tighter timing. If you cannot reliably cover any return window, investigate vacation mode and its current conditions before the absence. It is not an emergency button to assume will fix an already developing attack.

example.title: Illustrative schedule
example.text: You expect to be home at 18:00 but might be delayed 30 minutes. A landing at 18:05 is a poor plan. Select a route that gives you a comfortable margin after the latest realistic return, then confirm its exact timing in game. If your schedule changes, reassess before leaving rather than hoping the old plan still fits.

sections.title: Recall timing and threat response
paragraphs: Do one small deployment while you stay online. Inspect its outbound event, recall it, and observe the displayed return. Repeat with the ship mix you normally use, because the slowest ship affects travel. This is a route check, not a promise of invulnerability.

When threatened, first read the incoming mission and time. Do not recall in panic without checking whether you can cover the resulting return. Ask an experienced ally to review the precise situation privately. Do not publish live fleet coordinates or return times in a public alliance guide. After every save, inspect the original location for leftovers and new production.

sections.title: Match the mission to the exposure
paragraphs: Deployment remains the useful starting point because its outbound movement and recall have different visibility rules. With two suitable moons, a deployment avoids direct phalanx scans at both endpoints. Without moons, a deployment to another owned planet can be inspected at the receiving planet. Recalling removes that deployment from phalanx, but earlier scans may still help an observer estimate its return.

The important comparison is not simply moon versus planet. Check the mission, both endpoint types, which part of the flight is underway, and what happens if a moon disappears. The matrix below describes ordinary visibility before such changes.

sections.title: Two deployment routines, two commitments
paragraphs: An arrival save ends with ships stationed at the destination. Plan to be present before they land, with the destination inspected and the next move already affordable. This is the simpler routine to understand, but a visible destination arrival can become a target.

A planned recall save adds a second commitment: you must recall before the original arrival and then cover the newly displayed return. Decide on that window before departure. The best route is not the one that produces the longest flight; it is the one whose required actions you can reliably perform.

Practise with a small fleet while online. Record the displayed outbound arrival, recall it at a known time, and check the actual return. Do not use a generic stopwatch rule for a valuable fleet when the live event list can tell you the result. Changing research, bonuses, composition or speed can invalidate an old preset.

callout.title: After recall, the return is the commitment
callout.text: Do not assume you can recall a recalled fleet again. Confirm the new landing window immediately. Recalling simply because an attack looks frightening can exchange a manageable situation for a return you cannot supervise.

sections.title: When a moon disappears
paragraphs: Moon destruction can redirect a moon-related flight to the associated planet. That can create a scannable endpoint where none existed before. Re-read the event list after the loss instead of relying on the route you originally launched.

A player-recalled Deployment keeps its special phalanx treatment; do not apply that exception to every returning Transport, harvest or attack. Conversely, absence from a scan does not prove that an opponent lacks a return estimate. If someone observed the outbound Deployment and the moment it disappeared, they may have enough information to attempt a timed return hit.

Version caveat: a 22 September 2021 staff reply described a Deployment already en route from a planet to its own moon when the moon was destroyed: on reaching the missing destination, it automatically returned to the planet and became phalanx-visible. Live version 12.0.36, released on 27 March 2025, later included moon-loss Deployment visibility fixes, but its notes do not identify this exact same-coordinate case. The current-version behavior of that automatic return has not been verified. Do not assume an automatic return behaves like a player-initiated recall; recheck the actual route and landing.

The live March 2026 change slows Moon Destruction through a fixed Deathstar speed of 310, independent of normal server fleet speed and higher Hyperspace Drive. It buys time in some situations, not immunity. Other Deathstar missions use their normal speed rules. Check the incoming mission itself before estimating your response window.

sections.title: Prepare the landing, including everything left behind
steps: List the protected fleet, resources, outstanding returns and unfinished shipyard batches. Satellites, crawlers and defense are stationary assets and need their own protection and replacement plan.
Reserve enough fleet slots, local fuel and transport capacity for the next move. A fleet that has landed safely but cannot leave is still exposed.
Before logging off, reopen the event list and check the actual mission, planet/moon types, fleet composition and time. Inspect the launch location for ships or resources you missed.
Log in with a margin before the earliest relevant landing. Review all arrivals, not just the main fleet. Delayed expeditions and returning supply cargo may need separate handling.

If the schedule changes, reassess while there is still a choice. Plan longer absences ahead using the current vacation-mode conditions. Do not depend on an emergency setting to undo an attack already being resolved.

sections.title: What an expedition actually does

headers: What it means for your plan
rows: Income varies; resources need available cargo capacity
Dark Matter, items or other special finds
Separate reward rules; do not value everything as spendable metal
A normal possible result, not proof that the fleet is wrong
Combat can damage or destroy ships

Arrival can differ from the ordinary schedule

paragraphs: An expedition sends a fleet to position 16, holds there to explore, resolves an event and returns surviving ships. It is a chance-based income activity, not a raid on another player. Unlock Astrophysics 1 to start. Its baseline simultaneous-expedition allowance is floor(square root of Astrophysics): levels 1, 4, 9, 16 and 25 allow 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 respectively, before extra slots.

You also need an available ordinary fleet slot. Expedition capacity and total mission capacity are separate limits: an unused expedition allowance does not help when all fleet slots are busy. Discoverer, Admiral and slot items can add capacity; inspect the current totals before planning a batch.

sections.title: Build the slot count correctly
sections.body: The October 2026 administrator guide lists these additions to the Astrophysics-based expedition limit. Ordinary fleet slots are a separate constraint: having enough expedition slots does not guarantee enough free fleet slots to launch them. Recheck the displayed limit when bonuses or items expire.

rows: Different tiers can combine for +6 while active
For the active Discoverer; verify the current total

sections.title: Record the account you are calculating for
paragraphs: Expedition fleet recommendations are conditional. Record your class, economy speed, relevant research and lifeform bonuses, available expedition slots and the current top-player points bracket. These affect the useful fleet size or the number of missions you can run. The October 2026 OGame US administrator guide recommends a calculator instead of a fixed cargo count.

Verify that any calculator supports your current game version and modifiers. A mathematically precise answer based on the wrong class is still wrong. Save the input assumptions next to the result so you know when to recalculate.

Current-version support matters especially for non-Discoverer comparisons. October 2026 Orion test notes extended economy scaling to Collector and General. The November live rollout confirms version 13.1 but does not separately resolve that expedition change for every older universe. Do not present the old non-Discoverer formula as a universal current rule.

sections.title: Separate reward value from cargo capacity

example.title: Illustrative cargo check
example.text: If your current calculation permits a 12-million resource find but the selected fleet has only 8-million available cargo, that fleet cannot bring home all 12 million. Increasing capacity to cover the find solves that bottleneck. Increasing it to 30 million does not make the reward cap 30 million. Recalculate expedition value and cargo separately.

paragraphs: Two questions determine a useful fleet: is its expedition value sufficient for the relevant reward bracket, and can it carry the resource find? They are not the same statistic. The classic expedition points use base structural value, equivalent to the fleet’s Metal-plus-Crystal construction cost divided by 200; Armour Technology does not increase this build-value statistic. Above the useful point threshold, extra ships do not indefinitely raise the reward cap. Cargo capacity is a separate ceiling on what the returning ships can hold.

A Pathfinder provides the expedition reward multiplier described in the official guide; adding more Pathfinders does not repeatedly double that multiplier. More cargo can prevent a large find being truncated, but excess ships add fuel and loss exposure. A probe helps you read depletion, not multiply the reward.

sections.title: Build a replaceable working fleet
paragraphs: A practical starting concept is cargo capacity supported by a Pathfinder when available and an Espionage Probe for depletion information. The official guide also discusses a single strong combat ship for the find pool. Check the recommended composition against your unlocks and risk tolerance before copying it. Sending your entire battle fleet is not a substitute for calculating the expedition requirement.

Treat every expedition fleet as something you may lose. Keep essential transport ships and fleetsave capacity outside the expedition budget. If losing one launch would strand your account’s resources, make the working fleet smaller or build a replacement reserve first.

sections.title: Fleet verification before expansion
steps: Select an expedition destination at position 16 and confirm that the mission is Expedition. Review the selected ships and cargo capacity.
Choose holding time and speed together. Read the complete schedule and ensure you can cover a delayed return rather than only the normal one.
Launch a single test mission. Keep enough capacity and fuel at home for ordinary logistics.
Read the full report, including depletion information. Check the returning fleet and actual cargo rather than only the headline reward.
Only then fill additional expedition slots that fit your available attention and replacement budget.

callout.title: An expedition is not a guaranteed overnight fleetsave
callout.text: Events can delay the return or destroy ships. Keep your main fleet safety plan separate from your expedition income plan.

sections.title: Avoid the two common scheduling traps
paragraphs: The administrator guide states that longer holding time increases the chance of an event, not the maximum reward, and can increase delays. Do not extend a hold merely because you want a bigger payout. Depletion at a system’s position 16 is shared with other players; use reports to decide when to vary destinations.

The practical goal is a schedule you can repeat. A theoretically high number of launches means little if ships sit unattended after returning or you repeatedly miss your final collection. Plan the last batch backward from the time you want to stop playing, with room for disruption.

sections.title: Keep a simple performance log
sections.body: For a batch, record launches, elapsed time, resource finds, useful ship finds, fuel consumed and losses. Count ship value separately from spendable resources unless you have a realistic way to use or convert those ships. A large ship find does not automatically fund tomorrow’s crystal-heavy research.

example.title: Illustrative batch accounting
example.text: Twenty launches return 12 million resources, use 1 million in fuel and lose ships costing 3 million. The simplified net is 8 million resource units before any conversion assumptions. That is 400,000 per launch, not the 600,000 suggested by gross rewards. This example is bookkeeping, not an expected OGame return.

sections.title: Change one thing at a time
sections.body: Review a meaningful batch rather than reacting to a single black hole or exceptional reward. Change one input, such as cargo capacity or destination rotation, and note why. Recheck the calculation after class changes, substantial bonuses or a new points bracket. Do not spend your entire reserve chasing the best recent result. Stable logistics and the ability to replace a lost working fleet matter more than a spectacular screenshot.

sections.title: Keep the assumptions with the fleet recipe
paragraphs: A copied fleet count is useful only when its assumptions match yours. Record the universe and game version, player class, economy and peaceful-flight speeds, the top player’s points bracket, Hyperspace Technology, applicable Lifeform and class enhancements, actual ship cargo, slot bonuses and active expedition items.

Also record whether the calculator is sizing for the largest resource find, ship finds, or a smaller risk budget. Those are different objectives. Proxyforgame’s current page has separate resource, ship and class bonus inputs and a resource-discovery booster input; treating all of them as a single percentage can give the wrong answer. Its page currently identifies itself as OGame 13.0, so verify support for later changes before relying on a result.

sections.title: Value qualifies the fleet; cargo carries the result
paragraphs: The classic expedition-point calculation uses base ship structural value: combined Metal and Crystal divided by 200. Small Cargo contributes 20 points and Large Cargo 60. Armour Technology changes combat durability, not the base build value used for this calculation.

For a simple comparison, fifteen Small Cargos and five Large Cargos each cost 30,000 Metal plus 30,000 Crystal and each provide 300 expedition points. Before bonuses, however, their carrying spaces are 75,000 and 125,000. Equal points and equal construction cost therefore do not mean equal cargo. Speed, drive level, fuel and hostile encounters still need their own comparison.

Extra cargo can prevent a large resource find being truncated. Once both the useful expedition-value threshold and available carrying-space requirement are met, adding ships does not keep raising the same capped reward. It does increase the amount exposed to a full-fleet loss.

example.title: Translate a capacity target into ships
example.text: If a calculation requires 120,000,000 free carrying space and each Large Cargo actually contributes 37,500, the cargo-only quotient is 3,200 ships. That is a capacity calculation, not a complete expedition recipe: include support ships, loaded resources and the actual dispatch screen before treating it as a launch count.

sections.title: A baseline multiplier example, with its limits
paragraphs: The older official class FAQ gives a baseline Discoverer reward multiplier of 1.5 times economy speed, doubled again when at least one Pathfinder is present. Thus an eight-times-economy Discoverer with a Pathfinder has a baseline factor 24 before Lifeform or item modifiers. The Pathfinder factor is present once, rather than doubling again for each Pathfinder.

The archived table assigns a 5,000,000 Metal base maximum to the bracket above 100 million top-player points. In this deliberately unboosted example, 5,000,000 × 24 gives 120,000,000 Metal. This is a possible ceiling under those baseline assumptions, not an average find or a promise for a current account. A fresh universe may be in a much smaller bracket.

Do not reuse the old non-Discoverer multiplier as a universal live rule. October 2026 Orion test notes extended economy scaling to Collector and General. November’s live deployment announcements confirm version 13.1 and limit Orion activation to new universes, but do not separately document whether that expedition change is enabled on every older universe. Check the target universe and a supported calculation before making a class-switch comparison.

paragraphs: The Deathstar option belongs to advanced tradeoff analysis. Avoiding one event family does not turn an expedition into a safe place for irreplaceable ships. Compare extra cycle time and full-loss exposure before considering it; the ordinary cargo-led working fleet remains easier to replace.
Ship finds join the returning fleet; they are not a box of resources that automatically pays for the next upgrade. Keep usable ships, unwanted ships and resource income separate in your records.

sections.title: Turn slots and speed into actual daily launches
paragraphs: At Astrophysics 16, the baseline expedition allowance is 4. With Discoverer(+2), Admiral(+1) and an active Silver slot item(+2), the example allowance becomes 9, before other bonuses. Nine expeditions still need nine available ordinary fleet slots. Leave capacity for necessary transport, scouting and safety rather than discovering that the last launch has consumed all flexibility.

Expedition travel uses peaceful flight speed, but ordinary holding time is not divided by that speed. Plan total cycle time as outbound flight + selected hold + return flight, then add operational slack for events and for the time you are not online to relaunch.

For a simplified schedule, 20 minutes outbound + 60 minutes holding +20 minutes home is 100 minutes. Reducing each travel leg to 15 minutes makes 90 minutes, a 10% cycle reduction, not 25%. Over a continuous eight-hour window, the theoretical completed-cycle counts are 4 and 5. In a real workday, both may still yield only three launches if the return times fall between your logins. Buy the improvement your schedule can use.

sections.title: Treat risk, debris and events as separate systems
paragraphs: Expedition combat enemies scale with the expedition fleet, so adding military value also changes the encounter you may face. The October 2026 administrator guide reports a combat-debris cap of 20 million per resource type. This is not a guaranteed 60-million return, and resource eligibility and collection still matter. Older uncapped pirate-hunting plans should not be copied into a modern income routine.

A black hole can remove an entire working fleet. Keep the resources or ships needed to rebuild at least the amount of expedition capacity your plan depends on. If that reserve is unaffordable, a smaller fleet or fewer simultaneous launches may be a better choice than stretching to every slot.

Resource/ship bonuses, Dark Matter events, item-find limits and slot items are different mechanics. Read the current event announcement and expiry time. A nine-times-Dark-Matter event does not mean nine-times-resource finds, and a temporary extra slot creates a temporary operating opportunity rather than permanent capacity.

sections.title: Measure the operation without disguising its costs
paragraphs: Record launch count, resources by type, usable ship value, flight fuel, lost ships, actual cycle times and time left idle after return. Track losses even on days when the headline reward was unusually good. Decide on a consistent resource valuation before combining Metal, Crystal and Deuterium into one figure.

A useful performance record answers a decision: whether capacity is clipping finds, another slot can be used, a speed change creates an extra cycle, or a reward upgrade beats a mine project. It does not need a claim that one week establishes the true probability of a rare event.

example.title: A replacement reserve is a separate budget
example.text: If a working fleet costs 9 million planning units and you operate six, 54 million is exposed when all six are flying. Keeping 9 million available allows one immediate replacement, not six. That reserve is liquidity, not a deduction from every launch’s profit unless it is actually spent.

checklist: The reward calculation and free cargo both fit the target universe.
Every working fleet is replaceable.
The schedule and accounting include delays, fuel, losses and idle time.

guides.title: Moonshot budgeting and special cases
guides.summary: Keep debris math, probability, item handling and moon development separate.
guides.label: Detailed reference
guides.status: Evidence reviewed 9 November 2026. Historical formulas and unresolved live-version boundaries are labeled.
objectives: Keep debris math, probability, item handling and moon development separate.

sections.title: Choose the job before choosing the location
paragraphs: A moon is a separate location attached to a planet, with its own ships, resources and construction. It enables a Sensor Phalanx and, when paired with another owned moon, a Jump Gate. A planet can have one moon. You obtain it through a qualifying battle at that planet rather than by sending a Colony Ship.

Choose a location you will actually use: a collection hub, a route between your own locations, or a system from which phalanx coverage is valuable. Write down the purpose and the budget for developing the moon afterward. A moonshot that consumes all your transport capacity and fuel can leave the new location unusable.

sections.title: Size the battle for the universe you play
paragraphs: The conventional debris-based chance is one percentage point per complete 100,000 units of qualifying battle debris, capped at a 20% base chance. Use the debris produced by that battle, not old debris already at the coordinates. The standard target is therefore 2,000,000 debris. Event and Lifeform modifiers can raise the actual chance; 20% is not an absolute modern ceiling.

For an ordinary all-Light-Fighter shot, each destroyed fighter contributes 4,000 × f debris, where f is the ship-to-debris fraction. Required fighters = round up [2,000,000 ÷ (4,000 × f)]. This assumes all those fighters are destroyed and does not count extra losses on the receiving side. Simulate the exact battle.

example.title: A probability is not a promise
example.text: At a constant 20% chance, the probability of at least one success in n independent attempts is 1 − 0.8ⁿ. Five attempts give 67.23%; ten give 89.26%. Five failures do not make the next shot more likely. Set a maximum loss budget before trying again.

sections.title: Prepare a controlled moonshot
steps: Confirm the receiving planet has no moon, the debris setting, the current event window and the participants’ combat technologies. Agree on the exact coordinates, impact time, fleet composition and who will recover the debris.

Check the current rules for your community and universe before agreeing compensation. A friendly shot does not exempt transfers from pushing restrictions. If the arrangement is unclear, resolve it with support before the battle rather than relying on a years-old moonshot rule.

Simulate enough defending fleet or defense to destroy the intended shot. Include rapid fire, technologies and relevant bonuses. Move unrelated valuable ships and excess resources away from the receiving planet.
Arrange recycler capacity and timing, and keep the necessary defenders present until impact. A simulator estimates an outcome; the actual combat report determines what happened.
Inspect the combat report for the real chance and whether a moon formed. Reconcile debris recovery and agreed compensation. Stop or recalculate if losses or server settings differ from the plan.

sections.title: Read events and Lifeforms separately
paragraphs: Official events can advertise a 40% moon chance. For example, the OGame team announced one for 1–3 September 2026 and stated that M.O.O.N. items also received the event chance. That dated announcement is evidence of the modifier, not a claim that the event is running now. Check the current server announcement before choosing a date.

The Kaelesh Supra Refractor on the planet can improve the creation chance and the size of a newly created moon. The Origin Lifeform guide gives a maximum diameter of 9,400 km. It is not a Lunar Base upgrade and does not enlarge an existing moon. The community test linked below derives roughly 8,366–8,944 km for full-base unmodified shots; this is not an official guaranteed size range.

A 2025 community test thread also documents lunar-phase effects and corrects its own initial Supra Refractor chance formula. Treat such measurements as community evidence, not an official exact formula. Use the in-game building description and the combat report when planning a modified shot.

callout.title: Paid moonshots still need preparation
callout.text: M.O.O.N.S. items are optional, not guaranteed moons. Read the current warm-up, resource cost and conditions. Live version 13.0.0-r14 fixed the item fleets creating debris, so do not budget a recycler return from the paid item fleet. Ordinary player-organised shots use different debris handling.

sections.title: Reserve the field that creates the next fields
paragraphs: Without bonuses a new moon begins with one available building field. Each Lunar Base level adds three fields but uses one itself: the net gain is two. Before a size limit or other modifier, total developed capacity is 1 + 3 × Lunar Base level. Used fields include every Lunar Base level and the levels of other ordinary buildings.

At Base 3, the standard capacity is 10. Base 3 + Robotics 4 + Phalanx 1 + Jump Gate 1 uses 9, leaving one for Base 4. Filling that final field with another ordinary upgrade prevents the next Base until you free space or add an applicable field bonus. Check the displayed used/total count before every upgrade.

callout.title: Class fields can disappear
callout.text: General adds five moon fields while active. The official class guide states that switching away removes those extra fields but does not remove existing buildings, so a moon can become overfilled. Leave room for future construction instead of treating a temporary bonus as permanent.

sections.title: Build a small working base, then specialise
paragraphs: As a planning example, develop Lunar Base 1, Robotics 2, Lunar Base 2, Robotics 4 and Lunar Base 3. This leaves enough standard space for Phalanx 1 and Jump Gate 1 while retaining a field for the next Base. It is a field-safe sequence, not a mandatory optimum: if construction is slow, weigh another Robotics upgrade against the Base cost and your near-term objective.

Lunar Base starts at 20,000 Metal, 40,000 Crystal and 20,000 Deuterium, doubling for each successive level. Levels 1–3 together therefore cost 140,000 / 280,000 / 140,000. Budget resources for the other buildings separately. A Jump Gate requires a second completed gate elsewhere to do useful work.
steps: Build the Base and enough Robotics to make the next construction tolerable.
Choose whether the first useful tool is local phalanx coverage or a connection to an existing gate.
Add a Shipyard only when you have a specific local ship or defense requirement.
Recalculate free fields and construction cost before extending the plan.

sections.title: Supply the moon as its own location
paragraphs: Moons do not have a normal mining economy, and a planet’s Nanite Factory does not accelerate its moon. Bring construction resources, scan fuel and flight fuel from elsewhere. When dispatching to the same coordinates as the planet, explicitly select the moon destination type.

Use Transport when you want the cargo delivered and the ships to return. Use Deployment when you intend ships and cargo to remain there. Check both the arrival and the resulting return event. A convenient delivery time can still produce an inconvenient cargo-fleet return.

Storage buildings are generally a poor use of scarce moon fields: imported resources can exceed the normal production storage threshold. Do not build large stores merely to receive enough resources for a gate. Keep only the stock you need for planned operations and a deliberate emergency reserve.

sections.title: Protect the routine, not just the moon
paragraphs: A moon cannot itself be targeted by a Sensor Phalanx, but stationary ships can still be spied on and attacked. Moon-to-planet missions can expose information at the planet end. Learn the visibility rules in Moon tools and use the Fleetsaving guide to plan a return you can supervise.

Deathstars can destroy moons. Larger diameter makes destruction harder, but a large moon is not invulnerable. Loss of a moon can redirect relevant fleet movements to its planet, changing what an enemy can see. Avoid calling any unattended method completely safe.

Live version 12.9.0, rolled out on 26 March 2026, made Moon Destruction missions use fixed Deathstar speed 310, unaffected by higher Hyperspace Drive or server fleet-speed settings. Other Deathstar mission types retain their normal mechanics. Do not apply an old speed-universe moon-destruction timetable.

example.title: Before the first overnight save
example.text: Practise with a low-value fleet while online. Confirm origin and destination types, mission, payload, arrival or recall plan, and the time you must be present. Only scale up after you can explain what an opponent could observe at each end.

sections.title: Price the shot after recovery, not just before it
paragraphs: A conventional player-organised Light Fighter shot spends Metal and Crystal on ships and may recover part of that value as debris. The receiving fleet or defense can also suffer losses. Add those, fuel and recycler costs before comparing two arrangements. Agreed compensation is a separate transfer governed by the community’s rules.

At 50% ship debris, 1,000 destroyed Light Fighters cost 3,000,000 Metal and 1,000,000 Crystal and create 1,500,000 Metal plus 500,000 Crystal of debris. If that entire field is recovered for the operation, the shot’s unrecovered ship cost is 1,500,000 Metal plus 500,000 Crystal, before other losses or fuel. The 2,000,000 debris meets the ordinary 20% base target.

At 80% ship debris, 625 destroyed Light Fighters cost 1,875,000 Metal plus 625,000 Crystal and create 1,500,000 Metal plus 500,000 Crystal of debris. Recovering the entire field leaves 375,000 Metal plus 125,000 Crystal of unrecovered ship cost, before other losses and fuel. The same 2,000,000-debris target can therefore have a different replacement bill. The raw resource totals are not a value-equivalent planning sum.

sections.title: Distinguish the displayed chance from the debris target
paragraphs: A larger displayed chance can come from an event or another modifier, not only from more destroyed ships. Do not assume that a modified 20% report proves the battle generated the full 2,000,000 base-target debris. For the conventional full shot, retain the debris target as well as checking the modifier.

For an attempt that genuinely has a constant 40% success chance, three independent tries give 1 − 0.6³ =78.4% probability of at least one success. This is an illustration using a known 40% chance, not a method for calculating an event-plus-Lifeform chance. Each next attempt still has its own chance.

The public Supra Refractor guide and 2025 player tests support an effect on newly formed moon size, with 9400 km given as the maximum. The test thread corrects its initial chance equation, and the guide is marked as a draft. Keep precise stacking and rounding out of a guaranteed-cost claim unless current live evidence supports them. An existing moon does not grow merely because the planet later gains the building.

sections.title: M.O.O.N.S. items have different debris handling
paragraphs: A paid moonshot item is not equivalent to asking another player to send the same-looking fleet. The live 13.0.0-r14 notes explicitly fixed item fleets creating debris fields. Do not budget a recycler windfall from the item fleet or use its no-debris behavior to reinterpret ordinary player-organised moonshots.

Read the current item’s resource charge, delay and conditions before activating it, and prepare any defense needed for the attempt. Check the event announcement rather than assuming a past 40% event is still active. A chance-enhancing item or event is not a guarantee of a moon.

rows: Leave a field for the next Base.
A second completed owned Jump Gate
Both moons need fuel for ordinary flights.
Extra range matters only if it reaches relevant systems.
Shipyard and a narrow build plan
Moon fields and construction time are limited.
A larger moon purely for durability
Replacing a developed moon sacrifices its infrastructure and still leaves risk.

paragraphs: A moon’s best sequence depends on the network around it. A gate on the only moon cannot yet move anything, while a modest phalanx can already answer a local question. Equally, another phalanx level may be poor value if your purpose is simply to move cargo between distant collection hubs.

objectives: Plan ready gates, local fuel and phalanx information together.

sections.title: Unlock each tool for a specific job
paragraphs: Build these facilities on moons, not planets. Hyperspace Technology and Hyperspace Drive are different researches: the gate prerequisite is Technology 7. Open the technology tree before transporting a large construction budget.

Instant ship transfer between your own completed gates

callout.title: One gate is half a network
callout.text: Budget two functioning gates if you do not already own one. An ally’s gate is not your destination. Building a gate alone does not unlock transport to another player’s moon.

sections.title: Use a Jump Gate without stranding the fleet
steps: Confirm that the selected location is the origin moon, both gates are completed and ready, and the ships you need have actually landed there.
Inspect the destination moon before jumping. Put enough Deuterium there for the next ordinary flight, plus any reserve required by your plan.
Open the Jump Gate, select your destination moon and enter the ships to transfer. Check the quantities rather than assuming that every ship was selected.
Confirm the jump, then inspect the destination fleet and the origin’s remaining ships. The transfer is instantaneous and consumes no jump fuel.
Check the cooldown at both endpoints. If the next step is an attack, transport or fleetsave, dispatch it separately and verify its events.

callout.title: Ships travel; resources do not
callout.text: A gate cannot carry your Metal, Crystal or Deuterium. Jumping cargo ships does not move the stock stored on the origin moon. Arrange resource transport separately and keep its timing in your plan.

sections.title: Use the current cooldown, not an old wiki shortcut
paragraphs: Both endpoints enter cooldown after a jump. Published 2025 player measurements report 60 minutes at gate level 1 in a 1 × war-fleet-speed universe and 30 minutes at 2 × . These are observations, not an official timing formula: use both gates’ displayed ready timers. Higher gate levels reduce cooldown, but it is not simply 60 minutes divided by gate level.

The live 12.0.27 release on 23 January 2025 added the maximum effective upgrade level to the technology information. The updated description quoted on the official forum states level 9. The older Buildings tutorial’s level-15 / 10-minute claim is outdated.

Player measurements published in January 2025 found approximately 53:12 at level 2, 35:44 at level 5 and 19:29 at level 9 in 1 × war speed, with no further reduction above 9. These are reported observations, not an official exact timing formula. Use the actual ready timer for operations rather than a fitted polynomial.

callout.title: Plan both ends
callout.text: For an A → B → C route, B has just been used even if C is ready. Do not plan the second jump immediately. Recently relocated moons can also have a separate gate lock; inspect that status before committing a fleet to the route.

sections.title: Run a scan with a question in mind
paragraphs: A phalanx scan costs 5,000 Deuterium at the scanning moon. Select that moon, open Galaxy, locate an eligible planet and use the phalanx action. Interface labels differ between desktop and mobile. Read the mission, endpoints and server arrival time together; the timer alone is not enough.

Decide what you are trying to learn before paying: whether a particular arrival exists, whether the fleet is outbound or returning, or whether its timing has changed. Keep a manual record of the observation time when coordinating with allies. A scan is a snapshot, not a permanent subscription to the target’s movements.

example.title: Budget the information cost
example.text: Twelve scans cost 60,000 Deuterium. If the moon begins with 70,000 and you also need 20,000 for a flight, twelve scans would leave you short. Reserve operational fuel first, then decide how many observations the situation warrants.

sections.title: Calculate the basic coverage
paragraphs: Without class or Lifeform modifiers, range in systems to either side is L² − 1, where L is the Phalanx level. Level 1 therefore covers the moon’s own system, not zero planets. The total span on a sufficiently large non-wrapping map is 2 × range + 1 systems.
For a moon in 2:200, Phalanx 4 has base range 15 and covers systems 185 through 215 in galaxy 2, including both endpoints. It does not scan galaxy 1 or 3.

callout.title: Account and universe modifiers
callout.text: Discoverer has a +20% phalanx-range bonus, and Lifeform research such as Interplanetary Analysis Network can extend it. Use the displayed effective range for final eligibility; do not silently apply the unmodified table to a boosted account.

sections.title: Ask which planet can be scanned
paragraphs: Phalanx targets planets, not moons or debris fields. Visibility depends on the mission and the scanned endpoint. In particular, an outbound Deployment appears at its destination planet, not its origin; a recalled Deployment is absent from phalanx. Other returns to a planet can be visible at that planet.
This compact matrix describes the ordinary mission patterns. Moon destruction and redirection can change the endpoints, so reassess rather than treating the original route as permanent.

callout.title: Invisible does not mean unknowable
callout.text: An opponent may infer timing from earlier observations, debris disappearance or your routine. Phalanx immunity is one protection layer, not proof that a return time is secret.

links.description: Distinguish a player recall from the unverified current behavior of a same-coordinate automatic return.

sections.title: Account for the map and temporary restrictions
paragraphs: When circular solar systems are enabled, phalanx coverage wraps within the same galaxy. On a 499-system circular map, systems 499 and 1 are neighbours. A level-2 base range of 3 at system 499 covers 496, 497, 498, 499, 1, 2 and 3. Circular galaxies alone do not enable this system wrap, and phalanx does not cross a galaxy boundary.

Live version 9.2.1, on 9 March 2023, prevented a moon’s phalanx from being used while combat against that moon is being calculated. A failed scan at that moment does not establish that the target fleet vanished. Check the cause before changing a timed plan.

sections.title: Build an operating routine around the tools
steps: Before logging off, list every valuable fleet that will land, including cargo returning from supplying your moon network.
Keep a fuel reserve at the moons you expect to use. Do not depend on a gate to move resources in an emergency.
Check both gates’ availability and the destination’s fleet status before committing to a response. Gate mobility only helps after ships are present and the gate is ready.
Use moon-to-moon deployments as part of a considered fleetsave plan, with a return or recall you can supervise. Read the fleetsaving guide for the full procedure.
Follow current game rules. Do not use unapproved automation or attempts to obstruct another player’s phalanx or fleet controls.

example.title: A jump is not a fleetsave
example.text: If you jump to a remote moon and close the game, the ships are still stationary and attackable there. The useful question is not “Did I jump?” but “Where will my ships be while I am away, and when must I be present again?”

sections.title: The gate timer is local to the route
paragraphs: Both endpoints participate in a jump, so a ready third gate does not make a just-used middle gate ready again. Before a planned A → B → C move, check all three displayed timers and leave enough time for B’s cooldown.

Higher gate levels can be useful for a busy network. They are much less valuable when you use a moon once a day. Compare the next level’s cost, moon field and construction time with the actual minutes it saves on the endpoint that constrains you.

The current-description quotation identifies level 9 as the effective upgrade limit. Keep old level 15 claims and fitted cooldown polynomials out of dispatch planning. War fleet speed affects gate cooldown; economy speed and expedition peaceful speed are different settings. Use the ready display for the final decision.

sections.title: Keep a separate resource route
paragraphs: A gate transfers ships without jump fuel, but it does not carry Metal, Crystal or Deuterium. Supplying a moon and moving the combat fleet are therefore two separate jobs. If the cargo ships transport resources, they also create a return flight; if they deploy, the ships remain at the destination.

Keep enough fuel at each intended operating moon for the flight that follows the jump, including a safe departure if the original plan is cancelled. A remote gate with no flight fuel can move ships into a trap rather than solve a logistics problem.

An illustrative fuel reserve starts at 120,000 Deuterium. Planned scans require 30,000 and the next launch requires 70,000, leaving 20,000. If the emergency departure you want to preserve requires 40,000, the plan is 20,000 short before any surprise occurs. Reduce scans, supply more fuel or change the route first.

sections.title: A missing movement is a question, not a conclusion
paragraphs: A phalanx scan is a momentary observation of eligible movements. A movement can be absent because the mission is not visible at that endpoint, a Deployment was recalled, the fleet has landed, or the scan failed. These explanations require different responses.

Read the mission and endpoint types before converting a timer into an arrival claim. Do not infer cargo from the ship count, and do not treat a fleet’s absence on one planet as proof it returned safely to a moon.

For expensive or tightly timed decisions, preserve the observation time and recheck while action is still possible. Avoid unsupported guarantees about precisely how many seconds another player needs to escape; connection delay, interface state and server processing make those claims unreliable.

guides.title: Construction throughput and missile budgets
guides.summary: Use facilities to remove an actual bottleneck, with their side effects included.
guides.label: Detailed reference
guides.status: Evidence reviewed 9 November 2026. Historical formulas and unresolved live-version boundaries are labeled.
objectives: Use facilities to remove an actual bottleneck, with their side effects included.

sections.title: Unlock the capability you actually need
paragraphs: Nanite Factories and Missile Silos are planet facilities. Build them where their effect is needed; a Nanite on one planet does not accelerate another planet or its moon. The following are standard base costs before applicable modifiers. Facility costs double with each successive level.

callout.title: Capacity does not come preloaded
callout.text: An empty Silo provides no interception. After unlocking ABMs, you must actually build them in the defense production menu.

sections.title: What a Nanite Factory accelerates
paragraphs: Each completed Nanite level halves the standard construction time of buildings, ships and defense at that planet. Relative to Nanite 0, levels 1, 2, 3 and 4 give factors of 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and 1/16. It does not directly increase mine output or speed ordinary research.

Robotics affects building construction; Shipyard affects ships and defense. Keep these roles distinct when diagnosing a slow queue. A higher Robotics level is not a substitute for Shipyard levels when producing a fleet.

Schedule a Nanite upgrade around local production. An active ship/defense queue can block the upgrade from starting, and Nanite construction blocks those production jobs. Adding an order to a queue is not the same as its being able to start. Finish needed ABMs or emergency ships before taking that production capacity offline.
Lifeform construction can also conflict with Robotics/Nanite upgrades. Check which job is actually running: adding a queue entry is not the same as starting construction.

sections.title: Read a baseline construction calculation
paragraphs: For an ordinary building upgrade beyond the early-level speed-up, the baseline time in hours is (Metal + Crystal cost) ÷ [2,500 × (Robotics level + 1) × 2ᴺ × economy speed], where N is the already completed Nanite level. For ships and defense, use Shipyard level in place of Robotics. Deuterium cost is not part of this timing numerator.

The example assumes no Lifeform reductions, other modifiers or acceleration items. The game applies whole-second timing and minimum durations, so doubling a very fast facility is not necessarily useful for a unit already at the minimum. Use the displayed timer for the actual purchase.

callout.title: Do not apply this blindly to Lifeforms
callout.text: Lifeform buildings have their own scaling and modifiers. This table explains the classic construction factor; it is not a complete formula for every Lifeform building or technology.

sections.title: Buy time when time is the bottleneck
steps: List the next three construction or production jobs on the planet, their displayed durations and whether you can fund them.
Estimate how much of that schedule the next Nanite level saves. Include the Nanite’s own cost and the period during which its construction occupies or blocks local work.
Compare against the other bottleneck: if you wait days for resources and the queue is empty, faster production may not help immediately. If funded jobs are backed up, throughput has clear value.
Keep fuel, cargo replacement and essential defense reserves separate from the upgrade budget. Do not turn a convenience purchase into an unsafe transport situation.
When the upgrade completes, confirm its level and inspect the next job’s duration before filling a long queue. Record the result so that the next comparison uses your account’s actual modifiers.

example.title: A simple time comparison, not a resource-payback claim
example.text: Suppose the next funded work takes 48 hours at the current level. Halving it saves approximately 24 hours, but a Nanite upgrade occupying 30 hours would not make that short sequence finish earlier. A much longer funded backlog changes the answer. Earlier mine completion may also earn resources, which requires a separate production calculation.

sections.title: Reserve capacity for both missile types
paragraphs: A Silo provides 10 capacity units per level. One ABM uses one unit and one IPM uses two: ABM count + 2 × IPM count must not exceed 10 × Silo level. Upgrading the Silo increases capacity, not missile range.

Choose a defensive reserve before filling the rest with offensive missiles. Once ABMs intercept an attack they are consumed, so remaining stock matters more than the Silo’s level. The planet’s ABMs also protect its moon against IPMs; you cannot build a separate Silo on the moon.

rows: More offense means less interception reserve

callout.title: Do not demolish first and ask later
callout.text: The archived official guide requires an empty Silo before demolition. Removing stored missiles is a separate destructive decision; upgrading the Silo is possible without emptying it. Inspect the current control and consequences before clearing anything.

sections.title: Know what missiles destroy and what stops them
paragraphs: An ABM automatically destroys one incoming IPM and is itself consumed. Surviving IPMs attack defense, not the fleet or buildings. They ignore shields, and destroyed defenses do not receive the normal post-combat rebuilding chance. Attacker Weapons Technology and defender Armour Technology matter to the result.

Choose a primary defense type when launching. The aim is to remove a particular obstacle, not assume that one missile always destroys one turret. Use a current missile-capable simulator with the target’s technologies and defenses. Re-scout after impact before sending a fleet.

example.title: Interception comes before damage
example.text: If a planet has 12 ABMs and receives 20 IPMs, 12 missiles are intercepted and at most 8 reach the defenses, assuming no ABMs are added or consumed by another strike in the meantime. Those eight still need a damage calculation; “eight missiles” does not mean “eight Plasma Turrets destroyed”.

sections.title: Separate missile range from travel time
paragraphs: The standard range is 5 × Impulse Drive level − 1 systems, within the same galaxy. Impulse 6 reaches 29 systems either way. Where circular solar systems are enabled, measure across the shorter wraparound route. Circular galaxies do not let an IPM cross into another galaxy.

The archived Formula Thread gives the baseline flight time as 30 + 60 × system distance seconds, divided by the relevant fleet-speed factor. The Origin universe-settings guide classifies missile attacks as war missions. Thus, ten systems at × 2 war speed give a baseline 315 seconds, or 5 minutes 15 seconds.

callout.title: An archive inconsistency matters here
callout.text: The archived IPM Guide instead prints 30 + 30 × distance. Because the official archives disagree, this guide uses the Formula Thread baseline for explanation, not a guaranteed live countdown. Verify the game’s actual flight time before synchronising missiles with a fleet.

sections.title: Run a final check before launch
steps: Confirm the exact target, including planet versus moon, and obtain a recent report of defenses, ABMs and relevant technologies.
Check that the missile action is available from the intended source planet. Confirm range, stock, missile count and primary target.
Estimate the resource cost of intercepted missiles as well as those that reach defenses. Decide whether the resulting fleet operation still has a worthwhile objective.
Coordinate the timing if other strikes are involved, allowing for the defender rebuilding ABMs and for changes since your last report.
Read the final launch details carefully. IPMs cannot be recalled after launch. After impact, inspect the report and update the plan instead of repeating a salvo automatically.

callout.title: A Silo is a tool, not a safety guarantee
callout.text: ABMs do not stop attacking fleets or Moon Destruction missions. Keep your defense plan proportionate and continue fleetsaving; there is no building level that replaces supervision of valuable fleet returns.

sections.title: Include the upgrade interval in the schedule
paragraphs: The next Nanite level halves the remaining standard work you perform after it is completed; its own construction still takes time at the current level. When comparing a fixed funded backlog, let U be the upgrade duration and B the backlog’s current duration. Ignoring other interactions, upgrade-first takes U+B/2. It beats doing the backlog now only when B>2U.

If U=12 hours and B=40 hours, the upgrade-first sequence takes 32 hours and finishes 8 hours earlier. If B=16 hours, it takes 20 hours and finishes 4 hours later. This comparison values time only. Earlier mine income, future jobs, resource availability and using the upgrade to unlock something can justify a different choice.

Check Lifeform construction as well as the shipyard queue. Historical Lifeform changelog notes describe construction conflicts with Robotics/Nanite upgrades, while later interface fixes distinguish adding an entry from starting it. A queued Nanite icon is not proof that the upgrade is running. Complete urgent ABMs or cargo before starting a long local shutdown.

The cited Version 9 entries include beta and release-candidate notes, not separate proof of the current live deployment state. Check the present queue’s eligibility and technology information before scheduling conflicting work.

sections.title: Very fast production changes the comparison
paragraphs: Each classic Nanite level is a factor-of-two reduction before timing floors and other modifiers. Once a single unit is already at the game’s minimum displayed duration, do not assume another level doubles that unit’s practical throughput. Inspect the actual batch timer rather than extrapolating a long-job formula into the one-second range.

Choose a production test that resembles the future queue: the intended ship or defense type, realistic batch size and actual local bonuses. Another planet with different Shipyard or Lifeform facilities is not an interchangeable benchmark.

sections.title: Pay for the missiles that interception consumes
paragraphs: Twenty IPMs cost 250,000 Metal, 50,000 Crystal and 200,000 Deuterium. Against twelve ready ABMs, twelve IPMs are intercepted and at most eight reach defenses. Your budget still spent all twenty. Count that preparation cost when deciding whether the later fleet attack is worthwhile.

A defensive stock of twelve ABMs costs 96,000 Metal and 24,000 Deuterium. That comparison explains the value of a replenished interceptor reserve, but does not mean a small silo can defeat unlimited salvos. ABMs are consumed, replacements must finish, and the same planet’s stock covers its moon.

The existing capacity and range formulas are separate:10 capacity units per Silo level, ABM 1 unit, IPM 2 units; range 5 × Impulse−1 systems in the same galaxy. The old sources disagree on missile travel-time constants. Keep the displayed live countdown authoritative rather than publishing a synchronisation promise from either archive.

sections.title: Choose the operation before the salvo
steps: Identify what the missile strike is meant to remove and whether the follow-up still makes sense if the defender moves resources or adds ABMs.
Use a current report and include interception, technologies, target selection and the possibility of another player's simultaneous salvo.
Keep the planet and moon target types explicit. A planet’s ABMs can protect its moon, so a moon target does not bypass interception.
Check resource cost and actual stock immediately before launch. IPMs cannot be recalled after being sent.
Inspect the missile result and update the fleet simulation. Do not assume a fixed mixed-defense spillover order or automatic post-missile repair.

checklist: The funded backlog justifies the facility's cost and construction interval.
ABMs and IPMs fit shared capacity and have actually finished.

guides.title: Compare defense by cost and outcome
guides.summary: A reusable way to test a bunker without inventing a universal ratio.
guides.label: Detailed reference
guides.status: Evidence reviewed 9 November 2026. Historical formulas and unresolved live-version boundaries are labeled.
objectives: A reusable way to test a bunker without inventing a universal ratio.

sections.title: Make the routine raid unattractive
paragraphs: Start with a practical goal: protect the production that accumulates between collections, together with vulnerable stationary assets such as satellites and crawlers. Defense is fixed to its location. A stronger bunker does not make a parked fleet or a research savings bank safe, and it cannot replace fleetsaving.

Think like a raider. Their possible return includes loot and recoverable debris; their costs include lost ships, flight fuel and any missile preparation. Your job is to make ordinary attacks unattractive at the amount you actually leave behind. Even then, someone may attack for rivalry, military destruction or amusement. Unprofitability reduces an incentive; it does not grant immunity.

Defense does not slow an incoming fleet's timer. It may make an attacker choose a different fleet or abandon the idea, but once the attack is flying, your response window comes from the mission timing. Keep movable wealth mobile, collect regularly, and preserve fuel for leaving.

example.title: Budget for the collection gap
example.text: Suppose a planet produces 200,000 resources per hour and you normally collect every eight hours. That adds 1.6 million before your next visit. Test defense against that stock plus anything already parked there, not against an empty planet. A 24-hour absence raises the production component to 4.8 million. Changing your collection routine may cost less than buying enough defense for the longer gap. These are illustrative numbers, not a recommended safe stock level.

sections.title: Read the universe before choosing a build
paragraphs: Record the separate ship-debris and defense-debris percentages. Zero defense debris does not mean zero profit: your ships, satellites, crawlers and stored resources can still be the prize. In a defense-into-debris universe, the bunker itself can contribute to the attacker's return. Do not apply the ship percentage to defenses or calculate defense debris from gross battle casualties without checking the simulator's repair treatment.

Also record whether deuterium enters debris, hostile fleet speed, fuel consumption and ACS availability. Faster hostile fleets change your response window. ACS can change the scale of fleet that reaches you. After a merge or settings change, re-run your tests instead of assuming last month's defense target remains useful.

Use opponents that actually exist nearby. A layout tested only against cargo raids tells you little about cruisers, bombers, a mixed fleet or Deathstars. Keep those scenarios separate so you can see which threat the next investment addresses.

sections.title: Give each part of the defense a job
paragraphs: The cheap layer spreads random targeting across more units. Heavy guns supply stronger individual hits. That is a useful planning model, not a physical front line: an attacking shot can randomly hit a Plasma Turret even while thousands of Rocket Launchers remain. A large quantity of weak guns also cannot automatically overcome a shield threshold.
